**Message to Product Analyst** (request)

> Orrin Fieldworks (private; Salinas, California) — Series A, $18M at a $72M pre-money. Meridian Capital Ventures is deciding whether to lead with $12M. Read the attached client deck first (15 pages). Do not put any name from the deck into a web search; test the claims against the public literature and the competitor record.
>
> Your sections: 3 technology_product and 9 strategy.
> Decision question for section 3: has Orrin proved the picking technology under conditions that generalise to commercial fields, and is the IP strong enough to defend a $72M pre-money?
> 1) Map the published state of strawberry-picking robotics (peer trials, university extension trials, ag-robotics reviews): what pick rates, bruising rates and throughputs have independent groups reported, and how does 94% on 212 company-selected rows compare? Note the exclusions (plastic tunnels, standing water, slopes over 4%).
> 2) Is the 3.8% bruising / 2.1% unripe / 86% uptime bundle credible? What do horticultural studies say about bruising thresholds, shelf life and marketable yield, and what does hand-picking achieve?
> 3) Assess the IP: the patent landscape for soft grippers with slip sensing and stereo fruit detection; the significance of a first office action rejecting all claims; the value of two exclusively licensed university patent families; and the 2027-12-31 licence test at 100 robots.
> 4) Manufacturing: what BOM and contract-manufacturing evidence exists for ag robots at 300-500 units, and is $31,000-$33,000 plausible when the current build costs $48,000?
> 5) For section 9: is the RaaS plus engineering-services plus grant revenue mix a coherent path to a Series B, and what strategic options (OEM partnership, licensing, acquisition) exist? What does the 2027 plan of 360 robots require operationally?
>
> Counter-evidence to seek: independent trials below 80%, bruising above commercial thresholds, competitors already commercial in open field, patent prior art, contract-manufacturing quotes above plan.
> Peers: Advanced Farm Technologies, Harvest CROO Robotics, Tortuga AgTech, Agrobot, FFRobotics, MetoMotion, Dogtooth Technologies.
> Write 2,500-9,000 characters per section, 8+ figures, 4+ source IDs, with counter-evidence and diligence questions. Save your evidence blocks before drafting. Report back when both sections are saved.

Do not put any name from the deck into a web search; benchmark the terms against public comps and announced rounds.
>
> Your sections: 8 funding_valuation and 12 exit.
> Decision question for section 8: is $72M pre-money defensible against comparable rounds and precedent transactions, and what must be true for a Series A investor to earn a venture return?
> 1) Build the comparable-round set for agricultural robotics and automation: Advanced Farm Technologies, Tortuga AgTech, Harvest CROO Robotics, Agrobot, Carbon Robotics, Monarch Tractor, Burro, and any 2024-2026 rounds with disclosed revenue multiples or valuation step-ups. What multiple of ARR or revenue is $72M pre for $2.6M of 2026E revenue?
> 2) Public-market and M&A comps: Deere, CNH, Kubota, Trimble and ag-tech acquisitions (Deere/Blue River, Deere/Bear Flag, CNH/Raven, others). What revenue and EBITDA multiples have strategic buyers paid, and what exit value range is implied for a scaling robot company?
> 3) Stress the round: dilution from the note conversion and pool increase, the 1x non-participating preference stack across Series A, A-1 and Seed, and return math at plausible 2029-2031 exit values of $150M-$500M. What ownership and exit value does Meridian need?
> 4) Assess the terms against the market: 1x non-participating, broad-based weighted average, 8% non-cumulative dividends, a 5-seat board with one independent. Are these standard, and what protections should a lead demand (pro-rata, pay-to-play, information rights, tranching)?
> 5) For section 12: map the realistic exit universe (ag OEMs, robotics consolidators, private equity; an IPO is unlikely), precedent exit sizes and timing, and what the 2027 licence test and noteholder relationships do to exit options.
>
> Counter-evidence: ag-tech down rounds and failures (Abundant Robotics), hardware multiples below software, long adoption cycles, preference overhang.
> Write 2,500-9,000 characters per section, 8+ figures, 4+ source IDs. Save evidence blocks before drafting. Report back when both sections are saved.

**Message to Company Analyst** (request)

> Orrin Fieldworks (private, Delaware; HQ Salinas, California) — Series A, $18M at a $72M pre-money, target close 2026-12-15. Meridian Capital Ventures is deciding whether to lead with $12M. Read the attached client deck first (15 pages, figures as of 2026-09-30). Do not put any name from the deck into a web search; verify claims against public records by institution and role instead.
>
> Your sections: 1 company_overview and 2 team.
> Decision question for section 1: is Orrin a legally clean, properly capitalised Delaware parent that actually owns the fleet contracts and the IP, and what do the entities and cap table imply for a new lead investor?
> 1) Verify the Delaware incorporation date, good standing, registered agent, the California fleet LLC and the Mexican subsidiary, and whether the grower contracts sit inside the entity that borrows against the fleet.
> 2) Verify each founder's and executive's career and credentials against public records (university pages, patent inventorship, licensing, conference bios); flag any inflation or omission.
> 3) Is the 2023 CTO departure and the still-vacant CTO seat visible in public hiring, publications, litigation or corporate records? What execution risk does it create?
> 4) Do public records show liens, litigation, judgments or UCC filings against the parent or the fleet entity, and what related-party arrangements are disclosed?
> 5) Check the cap-table arithmetic: note conversion, option pool to 12%, the 1x preference stack and board seats. Is the pool adequate and is the note conversion correctly priced?
>
> Counter-evidence to seek: résumé inflation, undisclosed litigation or liens, an entity/asset mismatch, governance concentration, a thin bench behind two founders.
> Peers for context: Advanced Farm Technologies, Tortuga AgTech, Harvest CROO Robotics, Monarch Tractor.
> Lenses: state, federal and Mexican corporate registries and USPTO are material; the policy lens (farm labour, USMCA) belongs to the Regulatory Analyst.
> Write 2,500-9,000 characters per section with at least 8 figures and 4 source IDs; mark every claim resting only on the deck as verified/partially verified/unverified and include a claim-verification table. Save your section plans and evidence blocks before drafting. Report back when both sections are saved.

**Message to Regulatory Analyst** (request)

> Orrin Fieldworks (private; Delaware parent, Salinas, California HQ; Guadalajara, Mexico assembly) — Series A, $18M at a $72M pre-money. Meridian Capital Ventures is deciding whether to lead with $12M. Read the attached client deck (15 pages) first. Do not put any name from the deck into a web search; check the regulatory position against official sources.
>
> Your section: 13 esg, plus the regulatory and policy evidence the other sections cite (farm labour, trade, product safety).
> Decision question: which regulations and policies materially change Orrin's ability to sell, price and operate in California, Florida and Mexico, and what ESG liabilities should an investor price?
> 1) Farm labour: H-2A availability and adverse effect wage rates (DOL OFLC data), California wage orders and overtime thresholds, and 2025-2026 immigration enforcement. Is the labour scarcity that drives robot demand strengthening, and what would reverse it?
> 2) Mexico: USMCA rules of origin and the 2026 review, current US tariff treatment of robots and parts assembled in Guadalajara, and Mexican labour and environmental compliance for the subsidiary. What cost or market-access risk sits in the supply chain?
> 3) Product safety and liability: autonomous machinery operating around harvest crews, battery charging and transport, food-safety contact with fruit, and any Cal/OSHA, OSHA or FDA rules that apply. What liability regime and insurance requirements should the investor check?
> 4) Grants and subsidies: USDA SBIR Phase II compliance and reporting obligations (2024-2026), and whether public grant money creates audit or IP exposure.
> 5) ESG: agricultural labour practices, water and chemical use, and any disclosure regime that binds a private US company or its institutional investors. Is there a material ESG flag or is ESG not decision-changing?
>
> Counter-evidence to seek: rules that raise Orrin's liability or cost, food-safety concerns about machine-picked fruit, a policy shift that eases labour scarcity, trade barriers to Mexican assembly.
> Registries: DOL OFLC, USITC/USMCA, Cal/OSHA, FDA, USDA SBIR, USPTO where relevant.
> Write 2,500-9,000 characters for section 13, 8+ figures, 4+ source IDs, and file user data requests for anything behind a login. Save the evidence block before drafting. Report back when the section is saved.

**Message to Market Analyst** (request)

> Orrin Fieldworks (private; Salinas, California) — Series A, $18M at a $72M pre-money. Meridian Capital Ventures is deciding whether to lead with $12M. Read the attached client deck (15 pages) first. Do not put any name from the deck into a web search; verify the market and competitor claims against public data.
>
> Your sections: 4 market and 5 competition.
> Decision question for section 4: is the strawberry harvest-labour problem large and urgent enough to support the company's claimed $3.1B serviceable and $310M obtainable market by 2031, and does the bottom-up robot math hold?
> 1) Verify US strawberry acreage (the deck uses about 50,000 acres), the California/Florida split, season length, grower concentration and recent acreage trend from USDA NASS and the California Strawberry Commission. Is the acreage base shrinking?
> 2) Test the deck's bottom-up: 14,300 robots at one per 3.5 acres times $16,500 = $236M. Compare that with actual grower harvest-labour budgets per acre (extension cost studies, UC Davis, USDA) and with the $9,500-$12,700 prices the company actually gets. Is the obtainable-market number a share-of-wallet claim or a top-down hope?
> 3) What do H-2A data, California wage orders and farm labour surveys show about the labour gap and its trend? Does labour scarcity support adoption in 2027-2031?
> 4) For section 5: map real competitors by product (open-field, tabletop/greenhouse, harvest aids) with stage, funding, deployments, published pick rates and business model: Advanced Farm Technologies, Harvest CROO Robotics, Tortuga AgTech, Agrobot, FFRobotics, MetoMotion, Dogtooth Technologies, plus equipment makers adding picking arms. Is "the only autonomous open-field picker above 90%" defensible?
> 5) What is the base rate for agricultural robotics commercialisation — units sold, hectares covered, failures and acquisitions (Abundant Robotics, Root AI)? What does it imply for the 2% to 15% acreage adoption assumption?
>
> Counter-evidence to seek: declining strawberry acreage, low grower willingness to pay, competitors with larger commercial fleets, failed ag-robot scale-ups, a serviceable market smaller than claimed.
> Lenses: California and Florida are the revenue markets, Mexico the manufacturing base; note how season length changes robot utilisation and payback.

> **Findings that matter for the decision:**
> 1. The $310M obtainable market is arithmetically above the whole market: 50,000 acres / 3.5 x $16,500 = $235.7M at 100% adoption; $310M needs 132% of the US base. The deck's own 15%-by-2031 adoption yields $35.4M at list, $27.2M at renewal, and its 2%-by-2028 path conflicts with FY2028 revenue, which implies 7.1% adoption at $12,700.
> 2. Price is not the constraint: at list a robot-season equals 2-10% of the hand-labour bill it addresses, so adoption is gated by field quality (3.8% bruising; one Florida pilot exit), not willingness to pay.
> 3. Florida is counter-season capacity, not a stand-alone market: its 120-day season covers 2.0-2.5 acres per robot versus 3.5 in California. Mexico is a cost base only.
> 4. "Only picker above 90%" is a definition on company-chosen rows. Harvest CROO's 2025-04 claim, Advanced Farm's 2025 shutdown after a $25M Series B and Tortuga's sale to Oishii make the base rate failure or OEM absorption.
>
> **Notes:** answered the Product Analyst's note on competitor status; left one note to the Fundamentals Analyst on the FY2028 price assumption (782 versus 1,016 robots).
>
> **Open gaps:** NASS strawberry acreage, California Strawberry Commission data, H-2A certification/AEWR and the UC Davis harvest-cost study were not retrievable; four data requests are filed. Acreage and labour urgency remain unverified; confidence is high on the arithmetic, low on those inputs.

> The independent reviewer approved report version 3 (grade A, no Critical or Important item open), and it has been delivered as HTML and PDF with its source appendix. Data as of 2026-10-31.
>
> ## Rating: Wait for milestone — composite 4.1 / 10 (confidence: medium)
>
> **Action:** do not lead at $72M pre-money. Indicate $48M–$55M pre, with $6M now and $6M on 2027 milestones, subject to a Kestrel standstill and an independent harvest-level trial. Horizon: 6–12 months.
>
> ## Thesis
>
> The labour problem is real and Orrin has a working machine: five growers have paid for 75 robot-seasons and the California hand-pick wage floor fell to $16.90 in 2026 before AB 2646 restores $19.75 on 2027-01-01 — but the company's 94% pick rate is a share of *detected* ripe fruit on rows Orrin selected, and independent trials imply 75%–80% harvest-level recovery. At $72M pre-money (27.7x FY2026E revenue, 51.4x contracted 2027 robot revenue) the price already pays for the bull case; at $48M–$55M with tranching the same evidence pays for an option on a proven autonomy stack that an OEM would likely buy.
>
> It is not a Pass because the gating measurement is close and measurable: an independent trial, a firm v4 cost quote and a lender standstill could all arrive before the target close.
>
> ## Main risks
>
> 1. **Harvest-level recovery (most damaging).** 94% is conditional on detected fruit and selected rows; if detection is near 100% on unselected blocks the reprice is an expensive pass, if it is near 90% the robot is a harvest aid, not a crew replacement.
> 2. **Unit economics at the price actually charged.** 41% gross margin becomes −$8,100 contribution per robot-season at the $9,500 price once $12,000 of fleet depreciation is charged; the plan needs +74% price, −35% cost and −44% service cost simultaneously.
> 3. **Cash clock.** $3.29M gross at 2026-10-31, $1.79M usable above the $1.5M Kestrel minimum — 4.4 months to the covenant on 2027-03-14, before the 2027 season's first collections; only $4.0M of the $18M round is committed.
> 4. **IP and licence cliff.** Zero granted company patents, all gripper claims rejected, the PCT national-phase deadline passed on 2026-10-30, and the Calder licence lapses below 100 robots on 2027-12-31 (64 robots today).
> 5. **Entity/asset mismatch.** IP sits in the issuer, but the fleet, grower contracts and $1.6M of secured debt sit in Orrin Fleet Services LLC with no disclosed parent guarantee; in a sale the Series A may sit behind the lender.
> 6. **Concentration and market size.** 53% of 2026 paid seasons with two growers; Tallis is customer, contract manufacturer, noteholder and board observer (46% of FY2026E revenue); the claimed $310M obtainable market requires 132% of the observable $235.7M US robot pool.
>
> ## The one question
>
> **What is the harvest-level recovery rate — marketable berries in the clamshell divided by ripe berries on the plant — and the bruise rate against a hand-picked control, measured on blocks Orrin did not select?** At 75%–80% the price ceiling is a harvest-aid rental and the $310M market, the 360-robot plan and the $72M pre-money fall together; above 85% with clean bruising the same numbers become conservative and the round is financeable.
>
> ## Three takeaways
>
> 1. **Do not lead at $72M pre-money:** 27.7x FY2026E revenue and 51.4x contracted 2027 robot revenue price in the bull case; Meridian's 13.33% returns 1.67x at a $150M exit and 1.30x on the $116.8M probability-weighted value.
> 2. **Reprice to $48M–$55M with $6M now and $6M on 2027 milestones:** at $50M the assembled $16M round ($12M Meridian, $3.0M and $1.0M from the two co-investors) buys 18.18% of the $66M post and returns 2.27x at $150M and 3.79x at $250M; if the facility turns out to have no minimum-cash test, the bear weight falls from 50% to about 35% and this becomes Invest with conditions.
> 3. **The independent harvest-level trial is the gating measurement:** 75%–80% makes this a harvest aid, above 85% with clean bruising makes it a crew replacement.

## Final report

# Orrin Fieldworks: Investment research report
Rating: Wait for milestone
Composite score: 4.1
Data as of: 2026-10-31

## Executive Briefing

Orrin Fieldworks is a real machine in a real labour crisis and not an investable Series A at $72M pre-money. Five growers have paid for 75 robot-seasons, the California minimum wage rises to $17.40 in 2027, and the federal H-2A floor fell from $19.97 to $16.90 in 2026, with a court rejecting the 2026-08-03 rate method on 2026-08-26 and AB 2646 restoring $19.75 in 2027. An OEM will pay for a proven autonomy stack: Deere bought Blue River for $305M and Bear Flag for $250M. Against that, the 94% pick rate is a share of detected ripe fruit on rows Orrin chose, independent trials report 72%-87%, and the observable US robot-revenue pool is $235.7M at 100% adoption, not the $310M claimed. After $12,000 of fleet depreciation the unit loses $8,100 a season at the $9,500 actually charged, 56% of the $3.2M ARR is non-recurring or non-binding, and $1.79M of usable cash at 2026-10-31 is 4.4 months before the Kestrel covenant binds by 2027-03-14. Evidence confidence is medium-low: almost every operating figure is company-reported and unverified, and 20 data requests remain open [S53, S56, S181, S169, S190].

| Rating | Action | Composite score | Confidence | Horizon | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Wait for milestone | Do not lead at $72M pre-money; offer $48M-$55M with $6M now and $6M on 2027 milestones, subject to a Kestrel standstill and an independent harvest trial | 4.1 | Medium | 6-12 months, to the independent trial and the 2027 season | S53 unverified |

Our view differs from consensus on two measurements and on price, not on the existence of the problem. The consensus treats 90%+ pick accuracy, a $310M market and a $72M pre-money as proven; we find harvest-level recovery near 75%-80%, a $35.4M pool at the claimed 15% share rather than $310M, and the price at 27.7x FY2026E revenue against a listed ag peer median of 2.7x EV/Sales. At $72M Meridian's 13.33% returns 1.67x at a $150M exit, 2.78x at $250M and 1.30x on the $116.8M weighted value. At $48M-$55M the base case is the $16M round that assembles ($12M Meridian, $3.0M Granary, $1.0M Tallis): at $50M it buys 18.18% of the $66M post and returns 2.27x at $150M, 3.79x at $250M and 1.77x weighted; the full $18M (17.65%, 2.21x-3.68x) and a $12M-only close (19.35%, 2.42x-4.03x) bracket it. The scenario weights are 12% bull, 38% base and 50% bear; the bear is a lender event rather than dilution, because a close after Q1 2027 breaches the minimum-cash covenant around 2027-03-14. If the facility has no minimum-cash test, the bear falls to about 35% and the $48M-$55M structure becomes Invest with conditions [S53, S8, S14].

| Card | Text | Source |
|---|---|---|
| What it sells | 64 robots, 75 paid seasons and five paying growers at $9,500 a season in 2026 (company-reported, unverified); 110 robots contracted and 50 letters of intent for a 360-robot 2027 plan | S53 unverified |
| Performance | 94% of detected ripe fruit on 212 selected rows with 3.8% bruising and 86% uptime (company); independent trials report 72%-87%, putting harvest-level recovery near 75%-80% | S53 unverified, S56, S181 |
| Unit economics | 41% gross margin before $12,000 of fleet depreciation; contribution is -$8,100 per robot-season at $9,500 and -$650 at the $12,700 renewal with the $31,000 target cost; break-even is $13,350; a grower costs $300,000-$400,000 to acquire, so LTV:CAC is 1.1-1.6x at list | S53 unverified |
| Cash | $3.29M of cash at 2026-10-31, $1.79M usable, 4.4 months to the $1.5M Kestrel covenant on 2027-03-14; only $4.0M of the $18M round is committed | S53 unverified, S128 |
| IP and structure | No granted patents; all gripper claims rejected; the PCT national-phase deadline passed on 2026-10-30; the Calder licence lapses below 100 robots on 2027-12-31; fleet and grower contracts sit in a subsidiary with $1.6M of secured debt | S53 unverified, S128, S130 |
| Market | The US strawberry robot-revenue pool is $235.7M at 100% adoption and list price; the claimed $310M is 132% of it; 15% adoption by 2031 is $35.4M at list | S53 unverified |

The recommendation is Wait for milestone, not Pass: the milestone is measurable and close. An independent harvest-level trial on unselected blocks, a measured v4 unit cost at or below $33,000, 250 robots contracted at $12,700 or more and a Kestrel standstill would reopen the case; the first two could be delivered before the 2026-12-15 target close. On that evidence a $48M-$55M pre-money with $6M now and $6M tranched is the structure that pays for the option without paying for the bull case. If the trial shows harvest-level recovery above 85% with bruising no worse than hand-picked fruit, the right answer reverses and $72M is cheap [S53 unverified].

| Measure | Value | Source |
|---|---|---|
| FY2026E revenue | $2.6M, 46% Tallis engineering services and 13% grants | S53 unverified |
| 2026 RaaS revenue | $0.71M | S53 unverified |
| Gross margin | 41% as reported; -85% after fleet depreciation | S53 unverified |
| Contribution per robot-season | -$8,100 at $9,500; -$650 at $12,700 with $31,000 cost | S53 unverified |
| Net burn and runway | $410,000 a month; 4.4 usable months to covenant at 2026-10-31 | S53 unverified |
| Pre-money / FY2026E revenue | $72M / 27.7x | S53 unverified |
| Burn multiple | 7.0x FY2026; 5.9x FY2027 | S53 unverified |
| Capital raised | $20.5M of equity and notes raised to 2026-10-31; $38.5M including the proposed $18M Series A; $0.65M grant; $2.5M equipment facility with $1.6M drawn | S53 unverified |

What is the harvest-level recovery rate, marketable berries in the clamshell divided by ripe berries on the plant, and the bruise rate against a hand-picked control, measured on blocks Orrin did not select?

The answer decides whether the machine supplements a crew or replaces one. At 75%-80% the price ceiling is a harvest-aid rental and the $310M market, the 360-robot plan and the $72M pre-money fall together; above 85% with clean bruising the same numbers become conservative and the round is financeable [S53, S56].

1. Do not lead at $72M pre-money: 27.7x FY2026E revenue and 51.4x contracted 2027 robot revenue price in the bull case, and Meridian's 13.33% returns 1.67x at a $150M exit [S53 unverified].
2. Reprice to $48M-$55M with $6M now and $6M on 2027 milestones; at $50M the assembled $16M round buys 18.18% of the $66M post and returns 3.8x at a $250M exit, and without a minimum-cash covenant the case becomes Invest with conditions [S53 unverified].
3. The independent harvest-level trial is the gating measurement: 75%-80% makes this a harvest aid, while above 85% with clean bruising makes it a crew replacement [S53 unverified, S56, S181].

Diligence next: the independent trial, the firm Tallis quote at 300 units, the Kestrel agreement and UCC filings, the Calder assignment and change-of-control terms, grower contracts and renewal prices, insurer terms for product liability, and the corporate records that confirm entity and IP ownership. Until those arrive, the deck's operating and financial claims are unverified company material [S53, S128].

## Company Overview

Orrin looks like a clean three-entity group, but the Series A issuer owns the IP while its revenue contracts and 64-robot fleet sit in a pledged subsidiary, so a lead buys preferred in an IP holdco whose value is pledged and whose licence is contingent. There is no VIE and the arithmetic is consistent; the problem is unverified. No Delaware, California or Mexican registry extract, UCC filing or USPTO record could be retrieved. "Legally clean" is a closing condition, not a finding; company facts below are unverified unless marked [S53].

Orrin Fieldworks, Inc. is the issuer and IP holder: five pending applications and the Calder licence. The fleet, the grower contracts that generate RaaS revenue and the only secured debt sit in Orrin Fleet Services LLC, a California subsidiary formed 2023-11-02; a Mexican assembly company runs Guadalajara. No parent guarantee, intercompany IP licence, service agreement, Kestrel consent or change-of-control term is disclosed; the registry folio, deed and partner register are missing, so the 99%/1% split rests on the deck alone (unverified) [S53]. Economically, the split means recovery runs through the subsidiary first: in a sale or default the $1.6M drawn on the Kestrel facility is repaid from the fleet and its receivables before any value reaches the parent, then the $36.8M preference must clear before the Series A sees a dollar. The $12M lead therefore ranks behind $18.8M of seed and note money and a $2.5M secured facility, holds no direct claim on the revenue-generating assets without a guarantee or assignment, and is underwriting the licence and team, not the fleet. The strategic consequence: only a lower price or a condition precedent moving the contracts and IP into the issuer turns this into an investable structure, because the present map gives the preferred no path to the cash flows it pays for.

The IP estate is thin. The company owns no granted patent: US 17/902,118, the soft gripper, had every claim rejected and remains in prosecution after a 2026-05 response; US 18/655,430 awaits examination; the PCT/US2025/027761 national-phase deadline fell on 2026-10-30. The core perception IP is licensed from Calder: two granted families, exclusive for agricultural harvesting, at 2.5% royalty and $40,000 minimum; exclusivity lapses if fewer than 100 robots are in commercial service on 2027-12-31 — against 64 robots and 75 paid seasons today. The licence's term and duration are not disclosed: the deck gives the 2022-01-20 grant, royalty and exclusivity test but not expiry, renewal, termination or assignment. Prior art in slip grippers (US20220134579A1; US4605354A) makes the rejected claims a novelty problem (unverified) [S53, S128, S129, S130].

Cap table arithmetic checks; the terms are less reassuring. Fully diluted is 12,000,000 shares today and 15,272,108 pre-money; at $4.7145 that gives $72.0M, and adding 3,818,008 shares gives 19,090,116 and $90.0M post. The $7.77M of 2025 notes convert at 80% of the price ($3.7716) into 2,061,303 Series A-1 shares, and the 1,210,805-share pool top-up is charged to pre-money, so new money buys exactly 20.0%. The 2,290,805 shares (12.0% of post-money) are called the "unallocated option pool" on top of 1,560,000 granted options, a 20.2% total overhang against a 10-15% norm; if 12% includes grants, the reserve is overstated by 1,560,000 shares. The 1x non-participating preference stack is $36.77M, 40.9% of post-money, and ranks pari passu with the new Series A; if SAFEs carry a preference it reaches $39.3M (unverified) [S53].

Orrin sells a seasonal service, not a robot: the customer a strawberry grower, the buyer the harvest owner, the budget the harvest-labour line. It grows by converting pilots to paid robot-seasons — two in 2025, five paying growers in 2026 — and by raising price from $9,500 to $16,500 list ($12,700 renewal) in 2027; 2027 is a manufacturing and field-service problem. Related parties are disclosed: the COO's wholly owned Vashti Harvest Services received $310,000 in 2025-2026; Tallis is a $2.5M noteholder, a $1.2M-a-year services customer to 2027-06-30, the v4 contract manufacturer, a board observer and a $1.0M subscriber; Marisol Ridge Farms, the COO's employer until 2021, is the largest customer at 24 of 75 paid seasons. Five board seats go two to common, one to Seed, one to Series A and one vacant independent; the CEO is chair, so founders plus Granary control three of five (unverified) [S53].

Against peers, Orrin's capital is modest and its proof narrow. Monarch has raised over $220M, Advanced Farm $25M and Harvest Croo $10M; Abundant Robotics shut in 2021-06. Orrin has raised $20.5M and fielded 64 robots at 14 farms — more proof than most seed-stage peers, but the 2027 plan needs 360 robots, 5.6x, with nine field staff. The counter-case is ordinary: subsidiaries hold fleet assets, lenders take collateral, related-party terms can be market. The rebuttal is that good standing, lien scope, licence term and contract assignment cannot be verified from the deck, so each becomes a condition precedent rather than an assumption. The decision is therefore invest only with conditions that convert assertions into documents (unverified) [S53, S54, S91, S93, S94].

## Founding Team & Key Personnel

The founders have real fit — a perception scientist who wrote the licensed IP and a harvest operator who ran the anchor customer's crews — but the bench behind them is one non-executive VP deep, the CTO seat has been vacant since 2023-08-31, and no public record verifies a single CV line. On 2026-10-31 three claims were checked by institution and role: Calder University (CEO doctorate and inventorship), Marisol Ridge Farms (COO role) and Corvane Robotics (VP Engineering role). No university, patent or employer page matched, and Calder University has no public web presence, so the credentials are unverified company material, low confidence on dates [S53, S128].

Each career reads as an operating apprenticeship rather than a venture pedigree. Castellano worked at Calder University's Field Robotics Lab in 2016-2021, rising from research scientist to perception lead on the 2019-05 trials and the 2020 and 2022 patents, and previously spent 2010-2011 as a controls engineer at Tallis Agricultural Machinery; she joined Orrin as CEO and chair on 2021-09-14. Vashti worked at Seabright Produce Partners in 2006-2014, moved to Marisol Ridge Farms as director of harvest operations in 2014-2021, and joined as COO at incorporation. Hollander previously worked at Corvane Robotics in 2013-2024, rising to gripper engineering manager, and joined as VP Engineering in 2024-02. Achterberg worked at Verdant Crop Sciences in 2005-2025, leaving as regional sales director (West), and joined as VP Sales in 2025-06. Benedetti has worked as a fractional CFO at Ledgerline Partners since 2016 and joined Orrin's finance function in 2024-09. Month-level start dates before 2021 are not disclosed; each span is bounded by the next dated event and remains unverified company material [S53].

Castellano carries the technical story: PhD robotics (Calder University, 2016), MS mechanical engineering 2012, BS electrical engineering (Ridgemont State, 2010). Her inventor record is dated by the 2019-05 trials and two grants, from dockets CU-2017-031 (2020) and CU-2019-114 (2022), licensed to Orrin on 2022-01-20. She is named on 11 Calder filings, all assigned to the university, of which Orrin licenses two families; the deck does not enumerate the eleven application numbers and no USPTO record was retrievable, so title and the scope of the nine unlicensed filings remain open [S53, S128].

Vashti supplies the commercial half, and the traction is relationship-led, not repeatable third-party sales. Marisol Ridge, his employer until 2021-09, ran 18 robots in 2025, 24 in 2026 and has contracted 40 for 2027; Pajaro Bluff took 16 in 2026 and 30 for 2027. Two growers tied to him account for 53% of 2026 paid seasons, and his wholly owned Vashti Harvest Services received $310,000 in 2025-2026 for moving robots and night supervision (unverified) [S53].

The largest hole is technical leadership. Co-founder and CTO Dr. Soren Abernathy, who co-led the 2019-05 Calder trials and the 2021-09-14 incorporation, separated on 2023-08-31 — 38 months before this round — keeps 720,000 vested common shares (6.0% today, 3.8% after), and has no disclosed separation agreement, release, non-compete, board role or consulting term. Whether his invention assignments to the company were executed is not disclosed; no USPTO assignment record could be retrieved, and he is not named on the deck's five company applications. A departed co-founder who knows the stack is a reference, potential claimant and competitor; the seat stayed open through the v3 release in 2026-03 and the v4 filing of 2026-07-08 [S53, S128].

Below the founders the hires are specialists, not a scale bench, and the matrix reads the same way: technical depth and industry tenure are high, prior exits zero, and scaling and finance thin. Hollander has the most relevant CV — 11 years in gripper engineering — but no CTO title, disclosed equity or manufacturing-scale record; Achterberg brings 20 years of agricultural sales but runs a four-person team and five paying growers; Benedetti is a fractional CFO with no full-time finance lead at Orrin. None of the five leaders has a disclosed venture exit; only Castellano has raised capital at Orrin, $20.5M across pre-seed, seed and notes. The 2027 plan implies 360 robots with nine field-operations staff, about 45 technician-equivalents at one per eight robots, and no hiring plan. Peer context: Monarch has raised over $220M, Advanced Farm $25M and Harvest Croo $10M; Abundant Robotics shut in 2021-06 and Deere paid $250M for Bear Flag in 2021-08. Reference checks should verify Castellano's Calder role, Vashti's Marisol scope, Hollander's Corvane record, Achterberg's sales record, Benedetti's CPA licence and Abernathy's departure terms; non-founder pay and equity are not disclosed. We would not lead at this pre-money without a permanent CTO, a full-time CFO and a Kestrel estoppel; for an investor, a smaller, tranched check at a lower price is investable (company-provided, unverified) [S53, S54, S91, S92, S93].

## Technology & Product

Orrin has built a strawberry picker that works at night and five growers pay for it, but it has not shown the machine holds up on the acreage growers actually farm, and the patents that would defend a $72M pre-money are rejected, unpursued or licensed from a university [S53]. A 64-robot fleet proves the team can build and service hardware; a harvest rate that generalises and an enforceable estate are what would justify a software multiple. Orrin's figures are unverified.

### The 94% is a success rate on a sample Orrin chose

Pick rate divides berries picked by berries the vision system classified as ripe, removing every berry the cameras never saw [S56, S42]. On that definition Orrin reports 94% over 212 rows at 9 of 14 pilot farms, with tunnels, standing water and slopes above 4% excluded, on rows it chose. Independent work is lower: Washington State University's open-field harvester detected strawberries 80% of the time and picked 74% of ripe fruit with leaf-blowing fans at 20 seconds a berry. At 85% detection Orrin's recovery is 80%; after 3.8% bruising and 2.1% unripe picks, 75% reaches a clamshell — a supplement to a hand crew.

| Metric | Orrin, 2025 pilots | Independent trials | Source |
|---|---|---|---|
| Pick success | 94% of *detected* ripe fruit | 74% of ripe (WSU 2025); 83-87% (JFR 2025); 50-97.1% (JFR 2019) | S53 unverified, S56, S42, S57 |
| Cycle time | 5.6 s per berry per arm | 20 s per berry | S53 unverified, S56 |
| Bruising | 3.8% at pick, no control | none reported in field trials | S53 unverified, S50 |

### Bruising is the metric with no benchmark, and one grower has left over it

The 3.8% is measured at the moment of picking with no hand-picked control, so it sits on no scale. Bruising expresses over 24-72 hours and opens the fruit to grey mould; the literature treats mechanical damage as a leading loss driver in the fresh-fruit chain, yet no strawberry-robot field paper reports a bruise rate (S50). The counter-case is a grower: Grower E in Plant City, one of five paying growers in 2026, ended its pilot over bruising.

### The machine has no safety file, and the sanitation duty sits with the grower

Orrin discloses no conformity assessment, CE or UKCA marking, incident log or insurance terms (S53). ISO 18497-1:2024 sets design principles and vocabulary for autonomous farm machinery (S166), and ISO 18497-4:2024, published 2024-07-31, the verification and validation methods (S199); both are voluntary, and with no US federal rule on ground-based harvest robots, a worker injury would be argued as strict product liability, a jury setting the standard of care (S162). Food safety is nearer: the gripper, stem cutter and clamshell handler are food-contact surfaces, and 21 CFR 112.123 puts the duty to keep harvest equipment clean on the grower, not on Orrin [S163]; 32 US strawberry outbreaks sickened 933 people between 1997 and 2017 (S164). Cleanability is a requirement the buyer audits, and the 35% cost cut is where it is traded away.

### Uptime, supervision and unit economics that do not recover the robot

Orrin reports 86% uptime (unverified) over a 20-hour day: 2.8 hours of downtime per robot, or 22.4 robot-hours of attention per technician-day at 1:8 against an 8-10 hour shift — so either downtime is largely unattended or 1:8 is a best case. Depreciation is $12,000 per robot-season; 14% lost utilisation is $1,680, 43% of the $3,900 contribution claimed per robot-season. A real margin needs 74% more price ($16,500), 35% lower unit cost ($31,000) and 44% lower service cost ($1,750) at once; even then it is $12,250 against $7,750 of depreciation, 27% not 60% [S53].

### The IP is rented and no screened entrant touches the same claim

US 17/902,118 had every claim rejected in a first office action, with a response filed in May 2026, so there is no enforceable gripper claim today — an unresolved freedom-to-operate risk. Slip-sensing art dates to a 1986 US patent, so a narrow allowance is the best case. The perception that makes picking work is not Orrin's: two university families are licensed exclusively for agricultural harvesting at 2.5% of net robot revenue with a $40,000 minimum, and exclusivity lapses below 100 robots in commercial service on 2027-12-31. A funded 50-person team could match v3 picking in 24 months; matching a 300-robot service organisation takes four to six years, and it is where the best-funded peer failed (S114, S115).

Compared with Harvest CROO, which discloses no rate, price or fleet, Orrin's 64 robots are the category's only disclosed paid deployment. Three more entrants sharpen that read: none builds a soft-fruit end-effector, so none threatens freedom to operate in grippers or carries a picking claim against the 94%. AGRIST, founded in 2019 in Miyazaki, rents rail-guided greenhouse robots for peppers and cucumbers to Japanese co-operatives on a vendor-stated 55% harvest rate, after a 2025-09-17 Series B announcement (S183). Four Growers, with $15.1M raised, describes its greenhouse tomato robot as still in development, with two patents filed rather than granted (S185, S182). Carbon Robotics sells a laser weeder that never touches the crop, to roughly 100 growers on company figures, after $157M at its 2024-10 Series D (S184, S186, S55, S119). The robots that reached distribution avoid contact with the crop or run on rails, and each needed an order of magnitude more capital: a contact-based open-field picker remains the unproven category.

The denominator excludes undetected fruit; the sample excludes tunnels, standing water and slopes above 4%. Independent trials report 74% of ripe fruit at 20 seconds a berry (WSU, 2025) and 83-87% on detected fruit (JFR, 2025); recovery is 75-80%, the bruise rate has no comparator, ISO 18497 verification is absent and 21 CFR 112.123 puts cleaning on the grower. The screened entrants run on rails, work in greenhouses or never touch the crop. [S57]

Settling this needs detection on the same 212 rows, a bruise trial against hand-picked fruit (S53, S56), an ISO 18497-4 verification report and an ATP swab record (S163, S199). For an investor, the cheque should be conditioned on a licence renewal at $12,700 or more and a surviving claim.

## Market & Industry Analysis

The harvest-labour problem is real and the per-acre economics favour a machine, but the market numbers do not survive their own arithmetic: on the company's own figures, all 50,000 US strawberry acres are worth $235.7M of robot revenue a year at the 2027 list price, so the $310M "obtainable" market is 31% larger than 100% adoption of the entire US crop, on company-reported and unverified inputs [S53]. The strawberry opportunity is a $27-35M revenue business by 2031, not $310M, and field performance, not grower willingness to pay, is the binding constraint.

### Only one of the three market numbers is revenue

| SAM rebuilt: US strawberry robot revenue at 100% adoption | $235.7M (2027 list) | 50,000 acres / 3.5 x $16,500 | Derived from unverified inputs | S53 |
| SOM: claimed obtainable market | $310M (2031) | Needs 132% of the US base | Company target, unverified | S53 |
| SOM: implied by 15% adoption | $35.4M list; $27.2M renewal (2031) | 7,500 acres x $4,714 or $3,629 | Derived from unverified inputs | S53 |

Only the bottom-up sizes revenue, and it caps at $235.7M; the $42B and $3.1B figures are labour spend, unverified. Reaching $310M at list needs 18,788 robots on 65,758 acres, 132% of the US base; at the $12,700 renewal price, 171%. Management's 15%-by-2031 assumption gives 2,143 robots and $35.4M at list, 11% of the headline. At $3.1B it is 13.1x the strawberry robot-revenue pool, so it can only be soft-fruit labour spend; the deck does not say which acres fill the gap. The adoption path is unreconciled: 2% in 2028 is 1,000 acres, 286 robots and $4.7M at list, while FY2028 RaaS revenue of $12.9M at $12,700 implies 7.1% adoption; the implied CAGR from 2% to 15% is 96% a year [S53].

### The price is small against the labour it displaces

| Robot-season price | Price per acre | Picker-days at $180-$900 | Share of 896 picker-days | Status | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| $9,500 (2026 contract) | $2,714 | 11-53 | 1.2-5.9% | Unverified | S53 |
| $12,700 (2027 renewal) | $3,629 | 14-71 | 1.6-7.9% | Unverified | S53 |
| $16,500 (2027 list) | $4,714 | 18-92 | 2.0-10.2% | Unverified | S53 |

The picker-day equivalent follows from the deck's unverified productivity: a quarter-acre per picker-day is 14 picker-days per pass on 3.5 acres, and 1.5 acres per 24 hours at 20 hours and 86% uptime over a 210-day season is 64 passes. Willingness to pay is not the constraint; a machine that picked bruise-free fruit at that rate would be cheap at list. Buying only at the bottom of the ladder, and one Florida grower leaving over bruising, points to the real gate [S53].

### California's long season is the engine; Florida is counter-season capacity

| Region | Market size (year) | Growth | Company's position | Barriers | Key competitors | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| California: Salinas, Watsonville, Santa Maria | Part of 50,000 US acres (company, 2026, unverified) | US noncitrus bearing acreage -2% in 2025 | Entered: 4 paying growers; 53% of paid seasons with two | 7-month April-October season; AB 1066 overtime from 2022-01-01; tunnels, standing water and slopes above 4% excluded | Hand crews and H-2A; Harvest CROO | S53, S160, S141 |
| Florida: Plant City | Not disclosed | Not disclosed | Entered: 1 paying grower (11 robots); 1 pilot exited over bruising | 120-day December-March season (company assumption, unverified); 2.0-2.5 acres per robot | Harvest CROO | S53, S1 |
| Mexico: Jalisco | No robot revenue | n/a | Supplier only: 7 staff, gripper and harness assembly | USMCA sixth-anniversary review 2026-07-01; USTR 2027 review consultation 2026-10-02 | n/a | S53, S148, S150 |
| Europe and Australia | Not entered | n/a | IP optionality; PCT national phase due 2026-10-30, entry not disclosed | ISO 18497-1:2024; CE marking | MetoMotion, Dogtooth, Agrobot (tabletop, non-comparable) | S53, S151 |

California's seven months make one robot per 3.5 acres coherent: 1.5 acres per 24 hours over 210 days covers 226 acre-passes, 64 passes over 3.5 acres, picking every three to four days. Florida's 120-day December-March window, a company assumption with no public instrument setting it, covers 2.0-2.5 acres, so the same price implies $6,600-$8,250 an acre. Its value is utilisation: a robot in Florida in winter and California in summer logs two seasons and halves depreciation per season, but the 2027 plan prices 360 robots at $12,778 each for one paid season, so redeployment is not assumed. Mexico is a cost base, not a market. Of the eight market systems, three matter: home and revenue are California, the supplier base is Mexico, and the exit market is equipment makers, where Monarch Tractor, a $133M Series C announced by 2025-02-28 with over $220M raised, assigned assets for the benefit of creditors in January 2026 and sold them to Caterpillar in April 2026 [S54, S196].

### Who pays, and when

The budget owner is the grower's harvest manager, and the purchase is a seasonal rental agreed before planting for a season that runs April-October in California or December-March in Florida: one selling window a year, and a missed season costs twelve months. Concentration cuts both ways: a handful of California growers farm over half the state's acreage on the company's unverified estimate, and the paid book sits with two growers, one the COO's former employer. Few conversations decide the year, but the same buyers can resist the price rises the model needs.

### Policy is dated, and the wage floor fell in 2026

California AB 1066 (2016) put agricultural overtime on a 40-hour week from 2022-01-01 for employers with 26 or more employees, and the state minimum wage rose to $16.90 an hour on 2026-01-01. The H-2A adverse effect wage rate was $19.97 through 2025-10-01; the Department of Labor's interim final rule of 2025-10-02 (90 FR 47914) cut the operative California floor to $16.90 from 2026-01-01. The 2026-08-03 notice (91 FR 48946) set Skill I at $16.45 and Skill II at $18.71; the Eastern District of California held the methodology unlawful on 2026-08-26, leaving the rates in place with backpay possible; and AB 2646 restores a $19.75 floor from 2027-01-01. The USMCA sixth-anniversary review falls on 2026-07-01, and USTR opened consultation for the 2027 review on 2026-10-02, comments due 2027-01-12. ISO 18497-1:2024, published in 2024, sets the autonomous-machinery safety baseline for European entry [S141, S142, S190, S191, S193, S194, S195, S150, S148, S151]. Cheaper hand labour delays the annual purchase; the 2027 statutory rebound widens the saving.

### Shrinking acres and elastic labour are how this disappoints

USDA's 2025 noncitrus release reports 1.85M bearing acres across 21 crops, down 2% year on year, with strawberries among the three largest by utilised production; the strawberry line itself could not be retrieved, so the 50,000-acre base stays unverified. A 10% decline would cut the full-adoption ceiling by $23.6M and make 15% adoption harder. On labour, the floor fell in 2026 and rebounds by statute in 2027, and California's overtime rules raise peak-season cost only for larger employers. ERS's note that a warm spring brought an early 2026 California harvest shows that season timing, not only length, moves scheduling [S160, S169, S190, S161]. If guest-worker supply is elastic, urgency slips.

### What would settle it

Inputs that would move this from estimate to evidence are NASS strawberry bearing acreage by state, California Strawberry Commission grower and acreage data, and a third-party trial reporting detection and bruising against a hand-picked control. Stable acreage and a pick rate that holds without the row exclusions re-base the out-year line up; falling acreage with realised price near the current contract leaves the strawberry market small against the round. Confidence is high on the arithmetic and low on the acreage and labour inputs.

**The $310M obtainable market is 132% of the US strawberry acreage base at the company's own robot density and price, on company-reported figures that are unverified. (S53, unverified)**

Fifty thousand acres divided by 3.5 acres per robot is 14,286 robots; at $16,500 that is $235.7M at 100% adoption, against a claimed $310M obtainable market, all on company-reported, unverified inputs. The company's own 15% adoption by 2031 yields 2,143 robots and $35.4M at list, $27.2M at the renewal price. The gap needs acres outside strawberries or a price above list to close. (S53)

## Competitive Landscape

Orrin's claim to be the only autonomous open-field picker above 90% is company-reported, unverified, and its "only disclosed paid fleet" describes what rivals have not disclosed: DailyRobotics announced in November 2025 a first California deployment from April 2026, and Harvest CROO claims human-parity picking since 2025-04-24 [S53, S170, S1]. The question is whether Orrin turns a paid two-season lead into contracted acres before a rival closes it.

### One product, and only one of its three arenas is a robot market

| Competitor | Product and status at 2026-10-31 | Performance | Strengths vs Orrin | Weaknesses vs Orrin | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Hand crews and H-2A | Manual harvest; near-100% of US acres; H-2A floor $16.45-$18.71 (2026-08-03), $19.75 by statute from 2027-01-01 | Retail quality benchmark; no bruise rate | Proven quality, no capex, flexes | Wage floor fell in 2026; peak availability | S145, S141, S169 |
| Harvest CROO Robotics (Florida) | Open-field robot; 13 patents; commercial-viability claim 2025-04-24; no price or fleet disclosed | "On par with human harvesting" (company claim, unverified) | NSF SBIR tenure; Florida base; patents | No price, fleet or shipments | S1, S179 |
| DailyRobotics (Israel) | Q2 open-field unit, two arms, soft grippers; announced 2025-11 for California from April 2026; unconfirmed at 2026-10-31; RaaS, price not disclosed | About 30 kg/hour; 2-3x human speed (trade-reported, unverified) | Announced California entry; two-arm throughput | No confirmed deployment or acreage | S170, S198 |
| Advanced Farm (California) | Open-field strawberry and apple; commercial 2019; ceased operations 2025-07 | Not disclosed | Driscoll's and California Giant deployments; $25M Series B | Ceased operations | S93, S114 |
| Tortuga AgTech | Tabletop and greenhouse picking; sold to Oishii 2025-03-24 | Not disclosed | $47.7M raised | Non-comparable to open field | S115 |
| Academic and equipment makers | WSU and JFR prototypes; Deere and CNH sell no berry robot | 74-87% of ripe or detected fruit | Capital, dealers, acquisitions | Not commercial or not in this crop | S56, S42, S8, S95 |

The Picker competes in a hand-labour, harvest-aid and tabletop market; only the first is a robot market. The hand crew remains the default, harvest aids speed pickers without replacing them, and tabletop systems serve a different production system.

### The most dangerous competitor is the one with 100% share

A hand crew costs nothing when idle, needs no capital and meets the retailer's bar; Orrin must beat it on bruising before cost, and one Florida grower's exit shows the bar is real. Harvest CROO is the closest named threat: 13 patents, $10M over 14 rounds and a 2025-04-24 claim of human-parity trials. Its weakness is disclosure — no fleet, price or shipments — which is Orrin's opening: the first to show contracted acres at a real price sets the reference [S1, S179, S169].

### The 94% is a definition, not a barrier

The 94% divides berries picked by berries the vision system classified as ripe, so missed berries leave the denominator. The sample is on 212 rows at 9 of 14 pilot farms, excluding tunnels, standing water and slopes above 4%; it is company-reported and unverified. Independent systems publish 74% of ripe fruit at 20 seconds a berry and 83-87% of detected fruit. At 85% detection Orrin recovers 80%, and after 3.8% bruising and 2.1% unripe picks, 75% reaches a clamshell — a supplement to a crew, the conclusion WSU draws about its machine [S53, S56, S42, S57, S170].

### Entrants are screened out of the crop, not out of the threat

Three screened entrants do not compete in open-field strawberries. AGRIST rents rail-guided greenhouse robots for peppers and cucumbers after a Series B on 2025-09-17, at a vendor-stated 55% harvest rate and six Japanese deployments. Four Growers has raised $15.1M and calls its greenhouse tomato robot in development. Carbon Robotics sells a laser weeder that never touches the crop to about 100 growers; it raised a $70M Series D in 2024-10, $157M cumulative at that date, and $232M-$276M across two 2026 trackers with the $44M gap unresolved, unverified. None builds a soft-fruit end-effector, so the threat is capital and distribution; Orrin's $20.5M is 9% of Monarch's total [S183, S185, S182, S184, S186, S55, S119, S54].

### The moat is a service network, and the capital to build it sits elsewhere

The patents do not defend the position: every claim of the gripper application was rejected in a first action, with a May 2026 response, and the two perception families become non-exclusive below 100 robots in service on 2027-12-31, against 64 today. The barrier is a seasonal service network at one technician per eight robots. The open-source route moves fastest: a ROS 2 stack and published berry-perception literature remove an estimated 6-9 months from the 24-month estimate to match v3 picking, but supply none of the service organisation that takes four to six years. Monarch Tractor announced a $133M Series C on 2025-02-28 with over $220M raised to date, assigned assets for the benefit of creditors in January 2026 and sold them to Caterpillar in April 2026 [S54, S189, S168, S196, S181, S42, S56].

| Route | Months off the 24-month estimate | What it does not supply | Source |
|---|---|---|---|
| Open-source stack: ROS 2 manipulation, published berry datasets, general-purpose platform | 6-9 | Field service, grower contracts, fruit-quality validation | S181, S42, S56 |

### The base rate is failure or absorption, and the exits go to equipment makers

Abundant Robotics shut in 2021, Advanced Farm ceased in July 2025, Tortuga was absorbed by Oishii in March 2025, Traptic was acquired by Bowery Farming in February 2022, and Monarch's January 2026 assignment ended in a Caterpillar asset purchase in April 2026. The exits went to OEMs: Deere paid $305M for Blue River in 2017 and $250M for Bear Flag in 2021, CNH paid $2.1B for Raven in 2021, and AppHarvest paid $60M for Root AI. Deere's FY2025 10-K lists no berry robot, so the OEM threat is capital and acquisition appetite. That supports a trade sale, not an independent scale-up, and argues for pricing on contracted acres [S91, S92, S95, S196, S197, S114, S115, S8].

Orrin's wedge — RaaS, night picking, packing into the grower's clamshell and the COO's grower relationships — is real but narrow. For the investor, economics say scale, not invention, decides the winner, because whoever reaches contracted acres first sets the price reference, making an equipment-maker partnership the cheaper route. Orrin wins if fruit quality holds at scale in 2027 and renewals convert at the higher price; it loses if DailyRobotics confirms a California fleet, Harvest CROO shows contracted acres, or an equipment maker buys either.

**Orrin's "only open-field picker above 90%" and "only disclosed paid fleet" claims are company-reported and unverified, and the disclosure gap they rest on is closing: DailyRobotics announced a California launch for April 2026 and Harvest CROO claims human-parity picking. The 94% is a share of berries the vision system already classified as ripe, on rows Orrin chose, excluding tunnels, standing water and slopes above 4%; it is company-reported and unverified. ## Business Model

Orrin's robot-season is a fleet rental that loses $8,100 per unit once the robot is depreciated, so the company-reported 41% gross margin measures the wrong thing: at $9,500 the contract covers 54% of the fully loaded cost of a season, at the $12,700 renewal price 95%, and only at the unproven $16,500 list price does it clear cost. Five paying growers rented 75 robot-seasons in 2026 across a seven-month California season and a three-month Florida season; 14 farms have piloted since 2024 and 64 robots are in the fleet. Orrin Fleet Services LLC, a California subsidiary, owns, insures and maintains the robots, signs the grower contracts and borrows against the fleet, so the capital sits on Orrin's balance sheet, not the grower's. Payment timing, deposits and cancellation terms are not disclosed, so a collection after harvest could put the season's service bill ahead of its cash. Company-reported and unverified [S53].

The deck's own waterfall is $9,500 less $3,100 of field service and supervision (33%) and $2,500 of transport, insurance and consumables (26%), leaving $3,900 (41%). A v3 robot costs $48,000; straight-lined over four seasons, as the company does, depreciation is $12,000 a season. Charged to the contract, contribution is -$8,100 per robot-season, a gross margin of -85%; payback at $3,900 a season is 12.3 seasons, three times the depreciable life. Company-reported inputs; arithmetic verified against the deck [S53].

**The 41% gross margin is negative after fleet depreciation (company-reported, unverified).** $9,500 price less $3,100 of field service and $2,500 of transport, insurance and consumables leaves $3,900; a $48,000 v3 robot depreciated over four seasons adds $12,000, so contribution is -$8,100 per robot-season (-85%) and payback is 12.3 seasons against a four-season life [S53].

| $9,500 (2026 contract) | $48,000 (v3) | $12,000 | $5,600 | -$8,100 | 12.3 | Derived; unverified | S53 |
| $12,700 (2027 renewal) | $31,000 | $7,750 | $5,600 | -$650 | 4.4 | Derived; unverified | S53 |
| $12,700 | $31,000 | $7,750 | $4,250 (target service $1,750) | +$700 | 3.7 | Derived; unverified | S53 |
| $16,500 (2027 list) | $31,000 | $7,750 | $5,600 | +$3,150 | 2.8 | Derived; unverified | S53 |

### Only list price at target cost clears a season

At the $31,000 target cost the renewal price is the problem. $12,700 less $5,600 of direct cost leaves $7,100 against $7,750 of depreciation: -$650 a season and a 4.4-season payback that never arrives inside the asset's life. The fully loaded break-even price at current service cost is $13,350, so the renewal book is priced 5% below break-even; at the $1,750 target service cost it becomes $12,000 and the renewal earns $700 a season. At $16,500 the season earns $3,150 and pays back in 2.8 seasons, or $4,500 and 2.5 at target service. The deck's 2.1-season payback omits the $2,500 transport, insurance and consumables line; adding it gives 2.5-2.8 seasons, before any selling cost. The 110 contracted renewals, worth $1.4M, are therefore the weakest part of the book. A six-season life or Florida redeployment would halve depreciation and turn the renewal positive, but neither is in the deck. Company-reported prices; recomputed [S53].

### Concentration and lost deals carry the 2026 book

Of 75 paid seasons, Marisol Ridge Farms took 24 (32%) and Pajaro Bluff Growers Cooperative 16 (21%), 53% together; the COO was Marisol's director of harvest operations from 2014 to 2021. Counts partially verified; contracts unverified. Grower B cut from 22 robots in 2025 to 14 in 2026 (-36%) then contracted 20 for 2027 (+43%); its 2026 season record (acres, yield, bruising, uptime, price) is not disclosed and has been requested. An acreage or price cut leaves the renewal story intact; a performance or bruising cut from a reference grower contradicts it, and the 2027 increase to 20 favours acreage. The cut came in its second paid season while the paid fleet grew from 40 to 75 seasons. The 2027 book is an expansion bet on four of the five 2026 payers: their 110 contracted robots are 72% above the 64 they rented in 2026, and Grower D has no 2027 contract. The related-party layer compounds it: Vashti Harvest Services, owned by the COO, was paid $310,000 in 2025 and 2026 to move robots and supervise night shifts, and Tallis is at once the $1.2M services customer, a $2.5M noteholder, the v4 manufacturer, a board observer and a $1.0M investor. The ties are disclosed, but they mean concentration and service cost are not independent market evidence [S53].

### The KPI is seasons per robot, not robots sold

A robot-season is the unit of revenue, but the unit of cost is the robot-year: $12,000 of depreciation at the v3 cost and $7,750 at the v4 target, whether the robot works one season or two. In 2026, 64 robots produced 75 paid seasons, 1.17 seasons of paid revenue per robot. The 2027 plan's $4.6M of RaaS divided by 360 robots is $12,778 a robot, 23% below the $16,500 list and within 1% of the $12,700 renewal, which implies one paid season per robot and no Florida-to-California redeployment. If each robot served Florida in winter and California in summer, 360 robots could produce 720 seasons and halve depreciation per season, turning the renewal case positive; the deck does not claim it, and the $2,500 transport line and the absence of a 2027 Florida commitment suggest it is not yet operational. Overhead is the second KPI: FY2026 operating expenses of $6.9M over 75 paid seasons are $92,000 per season against a $9,500 price, falling to $30,000 at 360 robots in 2027. Until operating expense per season is below gross profit per season, more robots make the loss bigger. Customer acquisition cost is not reported: five sales staff at an estimated $180,000-240,000 fully loaded cost $0.9-1.2M a year; three new growers in 2026 imply $300,000-400,000 a grower, or $8,000-11,000 per contracted robot. At $16,500 a robot earns $12,600 over four seasons, so LTV:CAC is 1.1-1.6x and negative at renewal. Derived; unverified [S53].

| Monarch Tractor | $133M Series C announced 2025-02-28; over $220M raised; January 2026 assignment for the benefit of creditors; April 2026 Caterpillar asset purchase | Wound down; assets sold | S54, S196 |
| Carbon Robotics | $232M across five rounds | Private, 2026 | S55, S119 |

| Harvest CROO | $10M over 14 rounds | Private; demo 2025-04 | S94, S1 |
| Abundant Robotics | Not disclosed | Fruit-harvesting business shut down 2021 | S91 |

The peer record is one of large raises and two shutdowns: strawberry harvesting has absorbed substantial venture capital without a scaled commercial winner. The current contract destroys capital, the renewal price is below break-even, and the list price that works has not been sold. The counter-case is a six-season life, which cuts v3 depreciation to $8,000 and still leaves the 2026 contract at -$4,100, or a winter Florida season that halves depreciation per robot-year; neither is contracted, and both improve the renewal case without closing the overhead gap. The investor implication is to wait, or to tranche the lead check against the contracted fleet at list pricing and a v4 cost at or below target. Source: S53, S54, S196, S55, S91, S93, S94.

## Financial Analysis

Growth is not yet a robot business. FY2026E revenue of $2.6M splits into $0.71M of RaaS (27%), $0.34M of paid pilots (13%), $1.20M of engineering services to Tallis (46%) and $0.35M of USDA grants (13%); in FY2025 services and grants were $1.25M of $1.9M (66%). RaaS is 75 seasons at $9,500, the only line that scales with the fleet; the largest is a related-party engineering contract ending 2027-06-30, and the grant ends in 2026. Both disappear from the FY2027 plan, which is why projected revenue rises to $5.6M on $4.6M of RaaS. No audit exists and finance is part-time; FY2023-FY2026 are unverified management accounts [S53].

Reported gross margin rises from 53% in FY2025 to 58% in FY2026E and 61% in FY2028P, but mix flatters it. Removing $0.35M of grants, which carry little cost of revenue, leaves FY2026 gross margin at 51.1%; the RaaS line's own 41% is before $12,000 of annual depreciation per v3 robot, and after it the contract is at -85% (section 6). The $6.9M of FY2026 operating expenses is 2.65 times revenue and $92,000 per paid robot-season; at 360 robots in 2027, $10.8M of opex is $30,000 per season, 1.8 times the $16,500 list price. Even FY2028's $14.9M over 782-1,016 seasons is $14,700-19,000 per season, above gross profit at either price. FY2028 loses $6.9M. Unverified figures; verified ratios [S53].

The $3.2M ARR is not annual recurring revenue. It is $1.4M of contracted 2027 robot-seasons (110 robots at $12,700), $1.2M of Tallis services at an annual rate ending 2027-06-30, and $0.6M of signed, non-binding LOIs: 56% is non-recurring or non-binding, and only $0.6M of the services line will be recognised in FY2027. Against $0.71M of 2026 RaaS, $1.4M of one-season contracts makes $72M 22.5 times headline ARR but 51 times contracted robot revenue. The plan does not use list: $4.6M of FY2027 RaaS over 360 robots is $12,778, within 1% of the $12,700 renewal; after 110 renewals and 50 list-price LOIs ($2.22M), the other 200 robots average $11,900, 28% below list. The FY2028 line is stated at the $16,500 list — 782 robot-seasons, 2.2 times the 2027 fleet, 5.5% of 50,000 US strawberry acres — but on the renewal basis $12.9M needs 1,016 seasons, 2.8 times the fleet and 7.1% of acreage. Both exceed the 2% adoption the deck assumes for 2028 and need 422-656 new robots at $31,000-33,000, or $13.9-21.6M of unfunded capex. Split verified; contracts unverified [S53].

**The covenant rests on one deck line and leaves 4.4 usable months (company-reported, unverified).** Cash of $3.7M on 2026-09-30 is $3.29M on 2026-10-31 after $410k of burn and $2.68M at the 2026-12-15 close. This section uses usable months (cash above the $1.5M minimum divided by $410k) and labels gross months. Usable runway is 4.4 months from 2026-10-31 ($1.79M), reaching the minimum on 2027-03-14; gross runway is 8.0 months, to 2027-06-30. No facility agreement, UCC-1 or bank statement is in the register; the test rests only on deck p.10. If it does not exist, the 2027 failure mode is a 25-40% down round ($43-54M pre-money) rather than a secured-lender event, the bear weight falls from 50% to about 35%, and $48-55M becomes investable with conditions (tranche tied to contracted seasons, lender consent, no-default certificate). Source: S53.

The cash plan bridges the covenant. The $18M close plus $2.68M of cash at 2026-12-15 and $0.9M undrawn gives $21.6M; $9.9M builds 300 robots at $33,000, the FY2027 cash operating loss is $7.1M (the $7.9M net loss less $0.8M of depreciation), and an estimated $1-2M goes to working capital, leaving $2.6-3.6M at end-2027. Without the round, the dated $3.29M at 2026-10-31 less $2.46M of burn leaves $0.83M, and the $1.5M covenant is reached on 2027-03-14 first. At the $12M minimum close the same uses leave $1.4M short before working capital; it cannot fund 300 robots. The round buys one season, not a Series B. Burn multiple is 7.0 times in FY2026 ($4.9M burn over $0.7M of net new revenue) and 5.9 times in FY2027 (($7.9M loss plus $9.9M capex) over $3.0M of net new revenue); revenue per dollar of equity raised is $0.24 cumulatively and $0.15 on FY2027E. The $7.0M of 2025 notes convert at $7.77M into 2,061,303 Series A-1 shares at $3.7716, 80% of the $4.7145 price, and the $72M pre-money already includes that discount and the 12% pool. Company terms; derived bridge, unverified [S53].

Returns are below the cost of capital even in the target case. Fleet cash yield (contribution after depreciation over robot cost) is -16.9% at the 2026 price and $48,000 cost, -2.1% at the $12,700 renewal and $31,000 cost, and +10.2% at the $16,500 list and $31,000 cost, before $30,000 a season of 2027 overhead; Deere, the mature ag-equipment benchmark, earned a 17.5% operating margin and a 22.8% ROIC in FY2024. No balance sheet is disclosed, so DSO, DIO, DPO and goodwill cannot be calculated; the facts are $3.7M of cash at 2026-09-30 and $1.6M drawn, a net cash position of $2.1M ($1.69M at 2026-10-31) before the $1.5M minimum. Working capital is estimated: $2.0M of direct cost, $0.8-1.1M of receivables on $4.6M at 60-90 days, and $9.9M paid to Tallis before the season; grower and Tallis payment terms are not disclosed. Vashti Harvest Services, owned by the COO, received $310,000 in 2025-2026; warranty, capitalisation and revenue recognition are not disclosed. Company figures unverified; yields and working capital derived. Monarch raised $133M in its 2025 Series C and collapsed in 2026 [S53, S7, S54, S196].

Three cases bracket the outcome. Downside: only the 110 contracted robots deploy at $12,700, producing $1.4M of RaaS plus $0.4M of pilots, while $9.8M of operating loss and $9.9M of robot capex take usable cash below $1.5M in mid-2027. Base: the 110 contracts plus the 50 LOIs convert, producing $2.22M of RaaS; the company needs another round in 2027. Upside: 360 robots sell at the $16,500 list, producing $5.9M of RaaS, and FY2027 still loses $7.2M because $10.8M of opex exceeds gross profit at any price in the plan. Utilisation moves the outcome most: $10.8M of opex over 360 seasons is $30,000 a season, and break-even at list pricing needs 882-991 seasons, 2.4-2.8 times the planned fleet; $1,000 on 360 robots is $0.36M. Retention is second: Grower B cut from 22 robots in 2025 to 14 in 2026 (-36%), and its season record (acres, yield, bruising, uptime, price) is not disclosed and has been requested; an acreage or price cause leaves renewal intact, a performance cause contradicts it, and its 20 contracted 2027 robots (+43%) favour acreage. Grower D has no 2027 contract, Grower E exited over bruising, and four of five 2026 payers signed for 2027 (section 6). The 2027 milestone should be contracted seasons at list pricing and Florida-to-California redeployment, not robots built. Analyst estimates on unverified company figures [S53].

## Funding History & Valuation

At $72M pre-money Orrin is priced at 27.7x FY2026E revenue, 51.4x the $1.4M of contracted 2027 robot-seasons and 101.1x the $0.71M of RaaS revenue it billed in 2026; the multiple rests on unaudited company projections (unverified), and the round is defensible only as an option on the 2027 plan and an OEM exit of at least $270M, not as a price for the business that exists. At $50M pre the $16M round that assembles ($12M Meridian, $3.0M and $1.0M from the two co-investors) buys 18.18% of the $66M post and returns 2.27x at a $150M exit, 3.79x at $250M and 1.77x on the $116.8M weighted value; the full $18M buys 17.65% at 2.21x-3.68x and a $12M-only round 19.35% at 2.42x-4.03x [S53].

The $18M round at $72M pre implies a $90M post, 19,090,116 fully diluted shares and $4.7145 a share: new Series A 20.0%, the 2025 notes 10.8%, the unallocated pool 12.0%, granted options 8.2% — a 20.2% total overhang. At the deck's $72M pre, Granary's $3.0M and Tallis's $1.0M are new cash on the same terms and $4.7145 price as Meridian's $12M; the $7.77M of notes convert separately into Series A-1 (company deck, unverified). The pre-money already contains the notes' conversion at 80% of the price ($3.7716 a share) and a 1,210,805-share pool top-up, which transfers $1.95M to the noteholders and creates $5.71M of pool value; strip both out and the operating business sells at $64.3M-$66.3M. Orrin has raised $20.5M of equity and notes to 2026-10-31 and $38.5M including the proposed $18M round, plus a $650,000 SBIR grant and $2.5M of equipment debt. Cash is $3.7M at 2026-09-30 and $3.29M at 2026-10-31 at $410,000 monthly burn: $1.79M usable above the $1.5M Kestrel minimum-cash covenant, 4.4 usable months to 2027-03-14, or 9.0 gross months to zero from 2026-09-30. Peer disclosure is thin: Carbon Robotics has raised $232M, Monarch Tractor a $133M Series C announced by 2025-02-28 and Harvest CROO $10M over 14 rounds; Advanced Farm raised a $25M Series B in September 2021 with Kubota and Yamaha and ceased operations in July 2025, and Tortuga sold its IP, assets and team to Oishii in March 2025 [S53, S54, S55, S93, S114, S115, S119, S189]. None discloses a post-money valuation, so $72M cannot be triangulated against a peer multiple. No Mexican registry extract confirms Orrin Fieldworks Mexico, S. de R.L. de C.V. (Jalisco, formed 2024-07-19); the Calder licence term is not disclosed (unverified).
