The terms are conventional but incomplete. A 1x non-participating preference equal across Series A, A-1 and Seed, broad-based weighted-average anti-dilution and 8% non-cumulative dividends are standard; so is a five-seat board with two common seats, one Seed, one Series A and one independent agreed by both. Missing is the protection package: Meridian would hold one of five votes, with no disclosed protective provisions, pro-rata right, pay-to-play, tranching or information package, and Tallis holds an observer seat while also being a $2.5M noteholder, a $1.2M-a-year customer, the v4 contract manufacturer and a $1.0M investor (unverified) [S53]. The minimum package is a listed veto over budgets, debt, related-party contracts and change of control; pro-rata and pay-to-play; monthly fleet KPIs (robots in service, utilisation, pick rate, bruising, uptime, service cost, unit cost); and tranching of $6M against the 2027 season data.

What must be true is specific: 360 robots and $8M of ARR excluding Tallis services by 2027-12-31, the Calder licence still exclusive after its 100-robot test, unit cost below $36,000, and $67.5M-$84M of revenue at a 4x multiple by 2029-2031 (company plan, unverified). Deere paid $305M for Blue River (2017) and $250M for Bear Flag (2021), so a $250M-$300M technology exit is not fantasy. The counter-evidence is the category's own record: Advanced Farm, backed by Kubota and CNH, ceased operations in July 2025; Tortuga sold its assets; Abundant Robotics sold its IP in liquidation on 2021-06-29 [S91, S114, S115, S53]. At $72M the price discounts the strategic outcome and leaves nothing for the base case; a $48M-$55M pre-money, or $12M now with $6M released on 2027 milestones, is where the same thesis becomes an investment.

## Development Strategy

The revenue mix is a bridge rather than a business: in FY2025 engineering services for Tallis ($0.95M), USDA SBIR grants ($0.30M), RaaS ($0.38M) and paid pilots ($0.27M) made up $1.9M, so two-thirds came from work that does not scale with robots, and both non-robot lines stop by mid-2027. The FY2027 plan flips the mix to $4.6M of RaaS inside $5.6M of revenue, an 82% share, in a single season. The $3.2M "ARR" quoted to investors is a composite of $1.4M of contracted 2027 robot-seasons, $1.2M of the Tallis agreement at its annual rate — a contract that ends on 2027-06-30 — and $0.6M of signed letters of intent; on the definition a buyer would use, contracted recurring robot revenue is $1.4M, 51x at the $72M pre-money rather than the 22x the headline implies. The services line was rational at sub-scale; it is a valuation problem once the round is priced on recurring revenue. What the Series A must prove is that a rental fleet can be built, serviced and repriced inside one harvest season, and on the deck's own numbers — all company-reported and unverified in this review — the $16M the round actually assembles buys one season and 4.4 usable months to the covenant, not a path to a Series B. The plan asks the company to build, service, reprice and cost-reduce at once, all four in one four-month build window [S53].

### The round is $2M short of its own plan, and service labour is uncosted

A $12M cheque from Meridian on top of $3.0M committed by Granary and $1.0M by Tallis totals $16M, not the $18M the plan assumes, and the target close is 2026-12-15. The use of funds spends $9.9M on 300 robots at an average $33,000; the plan then loses $7.9M in FY2027 and $6.9M in FY2028 (company projection, unverified). Cash of $3.7M on 2026-09-30 is 9.0 gross months to zero at $410,000 of monthly net burn; the Kestrel facility, $1.6M drawn of $2.5M at 11.5% and secured on the fleet, requires $1.5M unrestricted at all times, so usable cash is $1.79M at 2026-10-31, 4.4 months, reaching the covenant on 2027-03-14, before the season's first collections: a close that slips past Q1 2027 is a default on the fleet, not only a dilution. The service side is worse than uncosted: at one technician per eight robots, 360 robots need 45 technicians against a field organisation of 9, and $1,750 a robot-season is $630,000 for the fleet, which does not cover 45 people at any California agricultural wage; either supervision reaches 1:25 through remote operation, which the 3.4 hours between interventions does not yet support, or the 52% gross margin is unavailable. The Series B in 2028 is not an option in this plan; it is an assumption [S53].

### Price the round, not the plan

The $16M the company can assemble is the case to underwrite, not the $18M plan. At a $50M pre-money with all $18M subscribed, Meridian's $12M buys 17.65% of a $68M post and returns 2.21x at a $150M exit and 3.68x at $250M; with the $16M — $12M from Meridian, $3.0M Granary and $1.0M Tallis — it buys 18.18% of $66M, returns 2.27x and 3.79x, and about 1.77x on the $116.8M probability-weighted exit value; as the only money it buys 19.35% of $62M, returns 2.42x and 4.03x, and leaves the 2027 plan $6M short [S53, S188]. The 2027 milestones below assume the full $18M: $9.9M of robot capex plus a $7.1M operating loss cannot be carried on $12M, so a $12M-only close moves the 300-robot build and the 360-robot season into 2028 and pushes the Series B back with them, while the $16M close funds the season with no reserve.

### The build and the related parties are the two ways this fails

Three hundred v4 robots must be delivered for an April 2027 season from a design never produced, assembled at a Guadalajara subsidiary with 7 staff, at a cost quoted by a company that is also the lender, an investor, a board observer and the largest customer (company-reported, unverified). The harvest calendar does not move, so a two-month slip is a lost season rather than deferred revenue; a company that has built 64 robots has a process but not a five-fold ramp. Governance compounds it. Tallis supplies 63% of FY2025 revenue as a customer, holds a $2.5M note, is committing $1.0M to this round and quoted the v4 bill of materials; the COO's own company was paid $310,000 for transport and night supervision; the COO's former employer is the largest grower customer, contracted for 40 robots in 2027; and two named growers are 53% of 2026 paid robot-seasons [S53]. None of that is improper, but neither revenue nor cost of goods has been tested at arm's length, and an arm's-length bid should be a closing condition.

### Three strategic routes, and only one is a fleet

The established route is an OEM partnership: CNH took a minority stake in Advanced Farm to co-develop harvesting, and Deere paid $250M for Bear Flag Robotics in 2021 and $305M for Blue River Technology in 2017; Deere's 2025 annual report makes autonomy central to its small-acreage strategy, where a berry picker fits. The second route is an asset sale: Tortuga's IP, assets and engineering team went to Oishii in March 2025. The third, licensing the perception and fleet-scheduling stack, collides with the Calder licence, exclusive only for agricultural harvesting. No standalone rental fleet at this scale has precedent: Harvest CROO has raised $10M over 14 rounds and remains private, Advanced Farm closed in 2025 after a $25M Series B, and the one field-robotics company at commercial distribution, Carbon Robotics, sells a laser weeder that never touches the crop, to roughly 100 growers, after $157M at its 2024-10 Series D [S117, S8, S114, S115, S184]. For Meridian the implication is structural: the cheque should buy an option on an OEM outcome, with contracts assignable and IP owned, not licensed.

### What must be true twelve months from closing

Five signposts, all company-reported and unverified until they appear in telemetry, decide whether a Series B is financeable. A 20-unit v4 pilot build before February 2027, with unit cost measured rather than quoted. At least 200 robots working by May 2027 rather than 360 announced. Renewals signed at $12,700 or more instead of the $9,500 of 2026. Uptime above 92% and a technician ratio near 1:20 shown in telemetry rather than in a slide. An independent harvest-level trial above 85% on blocks the company did not choose. The Calder 100-robot test on 2027-12-31 should be cleared by a wide margin under any credible plan, making it an early-warning indicator, not a live risk. Confidence in the arithmetic is high because every input is in the deck; confidence in the demand read-through is medium, because the 110 contracted robots sit with four growers, two related to the team, and the Florida season has already lost one customer [S53].

## Risk Assessment

Orrin fails on a dated financing clock before it fails on technology, and the $48M-$55M structure pays for that clock only if the lender has no minimum-cash test. The deck's $3.7M is dated 2026-09-30; at $410,000 a month it is $3.29M gross on 2026-10-31 and $1.79M usable after the $1.5M Kestrel minimum — 4.4 months, to 2027-03-14, with $4.0M of $18M committed against a 2026-12-15 close. The bull case needs six conjuncts: an $18M close in 45 days, a $31,000-$33,000 v4, 300 robots, 250 at list, 85% recovery and the licence test. The bear is one domino: a slipped round or a reprice, at 50-60% probability. With a minimum-cash test, bull 12%, base 38%, bear 50%, and failure is a secured-lender event; without one, 12/53/35, a 25%-40% down round, and $48M-$55M becomes Invest with conditions. No facility agreement, UCC-1 or bank statement is disclosed; the covenant rests on deck p.10, unverified [S53].

### Harvest-level recovery would break the thesis

The 94% divides berries picked by berries the vision system called ripe, on 212 rows at 9 of 14 farms, excluding tunnels, standing water, slopes over 4%; a company measurement, unverified. Independent machines report 74% of ripe fruit, 83-87% of detected, so at 85% detection harvest recovery is 80% before bruising, 75% after — and the 3.8% bruise rate has no hand-picked control, against a literature base rate of 78% severe bruising for mechanical blueberry harvest versus 23% by hand [S56]. At 75-80% recovery a fifth of ripe fruit stays on the plant, the same acreage needs 450 robots, not 360, and the price becomes a harvest-aid rental: the $235.7M pool, the 360-robot plan and any pre-money above $35M fall together. Even at full recovery unit economics fail: $9,500 a season less $3,100 service, $2,500 transport/insurance/consumables and $12,000 of fleet depreciation is -$8,100 per robot-season, and 56% of the $3.2M ARR is non-recurring or non-binding, leaving $1.4M of contracted robot revenue. That is -40% to -60% of enterprise value, the failure that turns a reprice into a pass.

**The thesis-breaking risk is that the machine is a harvest aid, not a crew replacement.** At 80% recovery the same acreage needs 450 robots, and every price assumes substitution. Source: S53, S56.

### The stress cases meet at the cash line

| Stress | What changes | Effect on the case | Source |

| Market 50% smaller (25,000 acres) | Pool $117.9M at list; 15% adoption gives $17.7M | $8M of 2031 ARR is 45% of that pool; $72M fails | S53, unverified; derived |
| Revenue 30% lower ($3.9M) | $0.87M less gross profit at 52% RaaS margin | End-2027 cash $0.6M-$2.6M; below the $1.5M minimum at the low end | S53, unverified; derived |

### The assets are split and the licence is not a moat

The issuer holds the patents and the Calder licence; the fleet, the grower contracts and the $1.6M Kestrel facility secured on it sit in Orrin Fleet Services LLC, with no parent guarantee or IP licence disclosed. Technology and fleet buyers would buy different companies, so 0-1.0x may be optimistic [S53, S128]. The licence cliff is narrower than it looks: non-exclusivity from 2027-12-31 does not stop Orrin operating; it removes a rival's barrier, so the impact lands on exit value, and 36 more robots clear it. The patent estate is thinner: every claim of US 17/902,118 was rejected (response 2026-05), and the platform PCT's national-phase deadline of 2026-10-30 passed with no entry disclosed, leaving Mexico, where the robots are built, unprotected.

### One counterparty is the revenue line and the factory

Tallis Agricultural Machinery is $1.2M of $2.6M FY2026E revenue (46%), the $2.5M noteholder, the v4 contract manufacturer, a board observer and a $1.0M investor, on a contract ending 2027-06-30. The Mexican subsidiary's 7 staff assemble grippers, not robots, so the 300-unit build has one supplier that is also its largest customer and creditor. Vashti Harvest Services, COO-owned, was paid $310,000 for robot movements and night supervision, inside the $3,100 service line that decides unit economics. The reference grower, Marisol Ridge (the COO's employer until 2021; 24 of 75 paid seasons), cut from 22 robots in 2025 to 14 in 2026 (-36%) in its second paid season while the paid fleet grew from 40 to 75 seasons; an acreage or price cut leaves the renewal story intact, a performance or bruising cut strengthens the bear, and with its 2026 record requested and not disclosed, the 12/38/50 weights stand (12/53/35 without the minimum-cash test) until it arrives. The ties are disclosed but unverified; the 41% margin and 53% concentration are not arm's-length [S53].

### The 2026 floor is 15.4% below 2025; 2027 adds a $19.75 statute

The $19.97 Farm Labor Survey AEWR governed through 2025-10-01; the Department of Labor's interim final rule 90 FR 47914 moved the operative floor to $16.90 from 2026-01-01 (-15.4%), and the 2026-08-03 notice 91 FR 48946 set Skill I at $16.45 and Skill II at $18.71, not the superseded $19.97. The E.D. Cal. ruling of 2026-08-26 left rates in place with backpay possible, and AB 2646 sets a $19.75 floor from 2027-01-01, 1.1% below the 2025 $19.97 and 16.9% above the 2026 $16.90. The risk is a one-season delay in an annual purchase, not a reprieve. The tariff is nearer: a 10% Section 301 duty on most Mexico-origin goods from 2026-07-24, USMCA-origin exempt, puts $3,300 on a $33,000 robot — $36,300 against the $36,000 ceiling — and $825 of extra depreciation that turns the -$650 renewal into -$1,475 [S190, S191, S193, S194, S195, S174].

### The category has killed better-funded entrants

DailyRobotics announced a first California deployment for 2026-04; unconfirmed at 2026-10-31. Monarch Tractor announced a $133M Series C on 2025-02-28 on over $220M raised, was assigned for the benefit of creditors in 2026-01 and sold its assets to Caterpillar in 2026-04; the category kills entrants with more capital than Orrin. Advanced Farm ceased operations in 2025-07 after a $25M Series B, and farm-robotics funding fell 36% Q2 to Q3 to $108M, 57% below a year earlier. A 2028 Series B is underwritten in a repriced market [S170, S198, S54, S196, S171].

### What to settle before signing

Four requests matter: the Kestrel loan agreement and UCC-1 (minimum-cash definition, cross-default, waiver price); the Calder licence (assignment, change of control, sub-licence); a fixed-price Tallis supply agreement; and an independent harvest trial on unselected blocks with a bruise control. Confidence is high on the cash arithmetic and tariff, medium on the covenant and harvest, low on the 2027 build and exit; the Kestrel text and Calder licence decide whether the bear returns capital or nothing.

## Investment Potential & Thesis

Orrin Fieldworks has built a night-picking strawberry machine that five growers have paid to use (company-reported, unverified), where the state minimum rose to $16.90 on 2026-01-01, overtime starts after eight hours, and the federal H-2A floor fell from $19.97 to $16.90 in 2026 before AB 2646 restores $19.75 on 2027-01-01 [S53, S141, S190, S195]. The need is real; the case is conditional. If the labour gap holds, harvest-level recovery proves above 85% with bruising no worse than hand-picked fruit, and the v4 lands at $31,000-$33,000 with service at $1,750 so the $12,700 renewal clears a $12,000 break-even, then 360 robots produce $4.6M of RaaS revenue and an OEM sale at $150M-$300M is credible. At $72M — 27.7x FY2026E revenue and 51.4x contracted 2027 RaaS — Meridian's 13.33% returns 1.67x at $150M and 3.33x at $300M. At $48M-$55M the base case is the $16M round that assembles ($12M Meridian, $3.0M Granary, $1.0M Tallis): at $50M it buys 18.18% of the $66M post and returns 2.27x at $150M, 3.79x at $250M and 1.77x weighted; the full $18M (17.65%, 2.21x-3.68x) and a $12M-only close (19.35%, 2.42x-4.03x) bracket it. Killer risks: negative contribution, a licence lapsing below 100 robots on 2027-12-31, and a lender covenant on 2027-03-14.

Consensus has the labour crisis creating a large, urgent market that Orrin leads: the deck claims the only open-field picker above 90%, a $310M obtainable market by 2031, a 41% gross margin, a 2.1-season payback, $3.2M of ARR and a $72M pre-money in line with peer rounds. We agree on the labour mechanism and disagree on two measurements. The 94% divides picked berries by berries the vision classified as ripe, on 212 rows at 9 of 14 farms it selected, excluding tunnels, standing water and slopes above 4%; independent work reports 74% of ripe fruit at 20 seconds a berry and 83%-87% of detected fruit, so harvest-level recovery is near 75%-80%. And the market is not $310M: 50,000 acres at one robot per 3.5 acres and $16,500 list is $235.7M at 100% adoption; the $310M claim is 132% of that pool. So: 41% gross margin becomes -85% after $12,000 of fleet depreciation, or -$8,100 per robot-season at the $9,500 charged, and 56% of the $3.2M ARR is non-recurring or non-binding. One trial settles the disagreement [S53, S56, S42, S57, S181].

The challenge moved probability mass to the bear: 12% bull, 38% base, 50% bear. The bull needs six conjuncts — v4 cost, 360 robots, 250 at list, an 85% trial, the licence test and an OEM or Series B — with $4.0M of $18M committed. The bear is one domino: a close after Q1 2027 breaches the Kestrel covenant around 2027-03-14, the v4 misses April 2027, the fleet stays below 100, and the Calder licence loses exclusivity on 2027-12-31. That 50% assumes the covenant exists; no loan agreement or UCC filing is registered. Without a minimum-cash test the failure is a 25%-40% down round, not a secured-lender event: bear about 35%, base 53%, and $48M-$55M becomes Invest with conditions. A 3-6-month reprice consumes the runway it protects; the standstill must be signed with the term sheet [S53, S169].

The technology exits; the company usually does not. Lely's Astronaut installed 50,000 units by 2024, 29 years after 1995, sold with dealer service — a seasonal-service adoption curve, not a software ramp. Deere paid $305M for Blue River in 2017 and $250M for Bear Flag in 2021; OEMs buy franchise-defending autonomy before revenue. The cautionary record dominates: Monarch Tractor announced a $133M Series C on 2025-02-28, raised over $220M, assigned its assets for creditors in January 2026 and sold them to Caterpillar in April 2026; Abundant Robotics raised $12M and liquidated in 2021; Advanced Farm closed in July 2025 despite Kubota and CNH backing; Tortuga sold its IP and team to Oishii in March 2025. Four of five funded peers failed or sold assets in 2021-2026 and none reached an IPO, so underwrite the $60M-$150M harvesting price, not the $305M headline [S177, S178, S92, S54, S189, S196, S91, S114, S115].

| Deere/Blue River | Best | 2017 | $305M for a 60-person pre-scale perception company; an OEM buys franchise-defending autonomy before revenue | S178 |
| Monarch Tractor | Cautionary | 2025-2026 | $133M Series C announced 2025-02-28; over $220M raised; creditors' assignment 2026-01, Caterpillar sale 2026-04 | S54, S189, S196 |
| Abundant Robotics | Cautionary | 2016-2021 | $12M raised and commercial apple trials, then liquidation; trials do not prove a business | S91 |

Three branches. Pass at $72M: the price capitalises a six-conjunct bull case and leaves 1.67x at a $150M exit. Wait for milestone, the recommendation: an independent harvest trial and a measured v4 unit cost, either before the 2026-12-15 close, move it. Invest with conditions at $48M-$55M pre-money: $6M now and $6M on 2027 milestones, with a Kestrel standstill, licence consent and entity consolidation as conditions precedent, not covenants. At $50M the assembled $16M round buys 18.18% of the $66M post and earns 2.27x at $150M, 3.79x at $250M and 1.77x on the $116.8M weighted value; the $18M and $12M-only cases give 2.21x-3.68x and 2.42x-4.03x. If harvest-level recovery is above 85% with clean bruising, the reprice is an expensive pass and the right answer is to pay up; that is the one result that reverses this recommendation. Open diligence would settle it: an independent trial on unselected blocks, a firm 300-unit quote, licence assignment and Kestrel consent terms, and fleet-entity consolidation [S53, S128].

## Exit Strategy Analysis

The realistic exit is a trade sale to an agricultural OEM in 2028-2031 at $150M-$300M; on the $116.8M probability-weighted value the $16M round that assembles at a $50M pre-money returns Meridian 1.77x (18.18% of the $66M post), against 1.30x on the same value at the current $72M pre-money; all 15 AgTech exits in Q3 2025 were M&A and none was an IPO, so the question is which OEM buys, when, and what the preference stack leaves [S187, S188].

Deere is the most plausible buyer: it has paid for autonomy three times — Blue River ($305M, 2017), Bear Flag ($250M, 2021) and GUSS Automation (2025) — but none of the three bought a harvesting robot: Blue River was see-and-spray and Bear Flag was tractor autonomy, both row-crop platforms that plug into Deere's dealer network. CNH's $2.1B for Raven was a $348.4M-revenue precision-ag platform at 6.0x sales, a scale deal rather than a technology option. The specialty-crop logic points to Kubota, which backed Advanced Farm's $25M Series B in September 2021 and watched it close in July 2025; CNH took a stake in the same company in 2022 [S96, S92, S8, S95, S93, S117, S114]. A closed portfolio company cuts both ways: it makes the next asset strategic and the buyer tougher on price.

The asset a buyer pays for is not the fleet. It is the ripeness model trained on 1.9 million berry images, the exclusive Calder University licence over two patent families with a 2.5% net-revenue royalty and a $40,000 annual minimum, the five paying growers and 75 paid robot-seasons, and the v4 design with its $31,000 target unit cost (unverified). That matters for timing: the licence becomes non-exclusive if fewer than 100 robots are in commercial service on 2027-12-31, the date that determines whether a buyer acquires an exclusive technology or a commodity one [S53]. A realistic sequence is a close on 2026-12-15, a first full season in 2027 with 360 robots and $8M of ARR, a Series B in 2028, and a trade sale in 2029-2031; the $1.5M minimum-cash covenant binds around 2027-03-14, before the season's first collections, so a close that slips past Q1 2027 turns a financing delay into a secured-lender event.

On those weights the expected company value is $116.8M; at 13.33% that is $15.6M, 1.30x, while the weighted average of the scenario multiples is 1.39x because the preference lifts the low-exit recoveries. The weights put 55% of outcomes at or below 1.0x, which is more generous than the 65% base rate for venture investments, because Orrin already has five paying growers; applying the base rate gives a lower expected value, not a higher one [S188, S53]. The modal successful outcome remains a $150M-$250M OEM sale, but a 30% failure tail at $10M — the category's own record — pulls the probability-weighted value below that range, and the preference stack caps the low-exit recovery.

Structure can block the buyer list. The Calder licence's term, assignment and change-of-control terms are not disclosed, and a university licensor can hold consent rights that delay or block a sale; the $1.6M Kestrel equipment facility is secured on the fleet, so the lender must consent to an asset sale or be repaid at closing; the noteholders' Series A-1 consent thresholds are not in the deck; and Tallis sits on five sides of the table as manufacturer, noteholder, customer, investor and board observer, so the v4 tooling and manufacturing agreement must be assigned to the buyer on terms the buyer accepts (unverified) [S53]. A foreign buyer such as Kubota also faces undisclosed licence-consent and export-control diligence, which could remove the most logical buyer.

| $72M (current) | $18M | 13.33% | $20.0M / 1.67x | $33.3M / 2.78x | $40.0M / 3.33x | S53 unverified |
| $50M (repriced) | $16M assembled | 18.18% | $27.3M / 2.27x | $45.5M / 3.79x | $54.5M / 4.55x | S53 unverified |

The entry price, not the exit, decides the return. At the current $72M pre-money, a $300M trade sale returns 3.33x, 27%-35% a year, and a $150M sale 1.67x, 11%-14% a year; at a $50M pre-money the same exits return 4.55x and 2.27x on the $16M that assembles, 4.41x and 2.21x on the full $18M, or 4.84x and 2.42x if Meridian's $12M is the only money. Liquidity is otherwise thin: the 8% dividend is non-cumulative, the company pays nothing before an exit, and a secondary buyer would discount a minority stake behind a $36.8M-$39.3M preference stack. The counter-case is that Deere, CNH and Kubota can build a picker in-house; the US strawberry-harvesting peer set has produced no disclosed venture-scale exit — Tortuga sold its IP, assets and engineering team to Oishii in March 2025, Advanced Farm ceased operations in July 2025, and Abundant Robotics sold its IP in liquidation after raising $12M — while the most recent harvesting-robot purchase, AppHarvest's $60M for Root AI in 2021, cleared at a fraction of the Blue River and Bear Flag prices. Hardware exits trade below software, ag-equipment multiples are 1.0x-4.3x sales, and the industrial sector ETF is down 6.9% over three months, 8.1 points behind the S&P 500, so a 2029-2031 window is not assured [S53, S115, S114, S91, S31]. Meridian should negotiate a drag-along and tag-along that make a trade sale executable without a founder veto, a right to consent to any change to the Calder licence or the Tallis manufacturing agreement, and a requirement that Kestrel be repaid or consented at closing.

## ESG Assessment

ESG does not decide this round, but three regulatory exposures do: a labour-policy tailwind that fell in 2026 and rebounds by statute in 2027, product-safety liability for autonomous machines working around crews, and USMCA origin risk plus governance conflicts that leave a new investor little control. Orrin is too small for ESG disclosure regimes to bind; what binds is the wage floor it sells against, the customs treatment of its Guadalajara assembly and its own safety and related-party terms.

### California's hand-pick wage floor fell in 2026; 2027 is the rebound year

California's hand-pick wage floor fell in 2026, not rose. The $19.97 Farm Labor Survey AEWR governed through 2025-10-01; on 2025-10-02 the Department of Labor's interim final rule (90 FR 47914) replaced it with two BLS OEWS tiers, $16.45 entry and $18.71 experienced, and the $16.90 state minimum became the operative floor on 2026-01-01, $3.07 (−15.4%) below 2025. By May 2026 about 70% of California H-2A employers had cut pay to $16.90, against a theoretical $100M saving on $655M of H-2A wages. The 2026-08-03 notice (91 FR 48946) refreshed the tiers at $16.45 and $18.71, not $19.97, the superseded 2025 rate. On 2026-08-26 the Eastern District of California held the methodology unlawful in UFW v. DOL, left the rates temporarily in place and raised backpay exposure. AB 2646 sets a $19.75 floor from 2027-01-01, COLA-indexed, +16.9% on $16.90. Non-H-2A growers saw a 2.4% rise, $16.50 to $16.90; H-2A crews saw about a 15% cut. No public California grower all-in hand-pick cost for both seasons was obtainable; $25-30 per worker-day of housing and transport means the all-in rate fell by less than the wage. Florida's entry rate fell 23.2%, $16.23 to $12.47. Confidence: high on rates, medium on all-in. [S142, S147, S190, S191, S192, S193, S194, S195]

### Trade: a 10% duty is small unless origin fails

Orrin's seven-staff Jalisco subsidiary assembles grippers and harnesses, and US entry turns on USMCA origin. Qualifying goods enter at 0%, while non-qualifying Mexico-origin goods face a 10% Section 301-type duty from 2026-07-24; machinery in HTS Chapters 84-85 generally needs 60% regional value content on transaction value or 50% on net cost. Ten percent of the $33,000 average v4 unit cost is $3,300 a robot, $990,000 across the 300-robot 2027 build. Trackers disagree: a 25% IEEPA duty or a 10% Section 122 charge from 2026-02-24. USTR opened consultation for the 2027 review on 2026-10-02, comments due 2027-01-12, and no outcome of the 1 July 2026 review was published. Make USMCA certification or a CBP ruling covering both the Guadalajara subassembly and the Tallis v4 build a closing condition. [S144, S148, S149, S150, S152, S156]

### Product safety is the liability that scales with the fleet

The Picker runs 20 hours a day, around harvest crews, on swappable battery packs. On company measurements it picked 94% of ripe fruit, bruised or punctured 3.8% and needed an intervention every 3.4 hours; one Florida grower ended its pilot over bruising. Food safety runs through the grower: the FDA Produce Safety Rule requires food-contact surfaces to be maintained and monitored, so cutting stems and carrying clamshells adds a surface to the grower's audit. ISO 18497-1:2024 sets design principles and vocabulary for autonomous machinery but certifies nothing, and Cal/OSHA has reviewed the family alongside an Australian code and EU Regulation 2023/1230. Liability is California strict product liability plus grower indemnity claims, and the only disclosed bucket that can absorb insurance is the $2,500 per robot-season line for transport, insurance and consumables, 26% of the $9,500 price. Diligence: limits, exclusions and incident logs. [S144, S151, S153, S154, S166]

### Governance is the clearest ESG flag

The company-reported, unverified related-party record outweighs any environmental metric. Vashti Harvest Services, wholly owned by the COO, received $310,000 in 2025-2026 to move robots and supervise night shifts, 16% of FY2025 revenue, while Tallis is simultaneously a $2.5M noteholder, a $1.2M-a-year engineering customer at 63% of FY2025 revenue, the quoted v4 manufacturer, a board observer and a $1.0M investor. Two of five seats are common, the independent seat is vacant, and the departed CTO holds 720,000 shares. Disclosure quality has an IP edge: every claim in application 17/902,118 was rejected in a first office action, with a response filed in 2026-05; the PCT national-phase deadline fell on 2026-10-30 while the October 2026 deck called it undecided. Hence the ask: an independent director, a related-party committee, monthly safety KPIs and inspection rights. [S144]

### Mexico, grants and disclosure are smaller but not zero

The Mexican subsidiary's seven staff sit inside IMSS social security, INFONAVIT housing contributions, aguinaldo and 10% PTU profit sharing, with dismissal without cause costing at least three months' salary plus seniority premium. The $650,000 USDA SBIR Phase II award, 16% of FY2025 revenue, carries Bayh-Dole obligations: a government licence, a US-manufacturing preference under 35 U.S.C. 204 and federal audit exposure, with counsel citing an executive order pushing agencies to take title and domestic manufacturing. If any Picker invention was made under the award, Guadalajara assembly may need a waiver. No mandatory climate or ESG regime binds a company of Orrin's size; LPs will extract reporting through side letters. ESG is not the binding constraint, except that governance and product-safety liability belong in the investment conditions. [S144, S155, S158, S159]

## Comprehensive Scoring & Recommendation

Orrin scores 4.1 out of 10 on the weighted table and the recommendation is Wait for milestone: the company has a real machine in a real labour crisis, but it is priced at $72M pre-money on unverified performance, negative unit contribution and 4.4 months of usable cash at 2026-10-31. The score reflects what can be proved today, not the technology. No independent source yet supports the technology or the financials, and 20 user data requests remain open, including the corporate filings, lender agreement and grower contracts [S53].

Technology and market carry the highest scores, and both stop at the same place. Technology scores 5 of 10: 64 robots and 75 paid seasons are company-reported, unverified, commercial activity, but the 94% is a share of detected ripe fruit on 212 rows Orrin chose, independent trials report 72%-87%, no granted patent protects the gripper, and the core perception is licensed until a 100-robot test on 2027-12-31 that the 64-robot fleet has not met. Market scores 6 of 10: the labour mechanism is real, with California's minimum at $16.90 from 2026-01-01 and $17.40 scheduled for 2027, and the H-2A floor cut from $19.97 to $16.90 in 2026 before AB 2646 restores $19.75 in 2027, but the robot-revenue pool is $235.7M at 100% adoption and the 15%-by-2031 case is $35.4M at list and $27.2M at renewal. A dimension without a peer benchmark scores at most 7; neither of these has a benchmark that supports more than 6 [S53, S56, S141, S190].

Three dimensions drag the composite into weak territory. Business model scores 3 of 10: at $9,500 a season the unit is -$8,100 after $12,000 of fleet depreciation, the $12,700 renewal is -$650 even at the $31,000 target cost, and only the unsold $16,500 list clears the $13,350 break-even. A grower costs $300,000-$400,000 to acquire, $8,000-$11,000 per contracted robot, so LTV:CAC is 1.1-1.6x at list and negative at renewal. Financial position scores 3: of $3.29M of cash at 2026-10-31, $1.79M is usable, the Kestrel $1.5M minimum-cash covenant binds by 2027-03-14, 46% of FY2026E revenue (company figures, unverified) is one related-party services contract and 13% is grants, and 56% of the $3.2M ARR is non-recurring or non-binding. Valuation scores 2: $72M pre-money is 27.7x FY2026E revenue and 51.4x contracted 2027 RaaS against a listed ag peer median of 2.7x EV/Sales and CNH/Raven at 6.0x, the 1x preference stack is $36.8M, or 40.9% of the $90M post, and the round carries no disclosed protective provisions. The covenant rests on the deck alone; without that test the 2027 failure is a 25%-40% down round, the bear weight falls to about 35%, and $48M-$55M becomes Invest with conditions [S53, S8, S12, S14, S95, S128].

Team scores 5 and exit 4. The founders have genuine domain fit, with the CEO writing the licensed perception work and the COO having run crews (company-reported), but the CTO seat has been vacant since 2023-08-31, no leader has a disclosed exit, nine field staff must become 45 technician-equivalents by 2027, and the CFO is part-time. The exit record cuts both ways: Deere paid $305M for Blue River and $250M for Bear Flag, but Root AI cleared at $60M in harvesting, and four of the five funded peers failed or sold assets between 2021 and 2026, including Monarch Tractor ($133M Series C announced 2025-02-28; assets sold to Caterpillar in April 2026); weighted across five outcomes the company is worth $116.8M, 1.30x at $72M (1.39x as the weighted average of scenario multiples) [S53, S178, S93, S54, S189, S196, S91].

| 5 | Labour policy | AB 2646 restores $19.75 on 2027-01-01; no H-2A expansion | A larger H-2A cap, an AEWR freeze, or backpay under the 2026-08-26 ruling | -15% to -20% | medium | DOL rulemaking on H-2A wages | S190, S195 |

The five key assumptions are ranked below, and the sensitivity of value to each sits in the impact column; the recommendation changes under the downside cases, not by dilution. A market 50% smaller, at 25,000 acres, gives a $117.9M pool at list and $17.7M at 15% adoption, which kills $72M but leaves $48M-$55M defensible. Revenue 30% lower, at $3.9M instead of $5.6M, removes $0.87M of gross profit at a 52% RaaS margin and leaves end-2027 cash at $0.6M-$2.6M against a $1.5M covenant, breached at the low end. Customer acquisition at twice the plan cannot be absorbed: 200 uncontracted robots have one selling window, four sales staff and a 5-of-14 pilot conversion record. Financing six months late adds $2.46M of burn and leaves $0.83M of cash on 2027-06-15, a secured-lender default rather than a down round. Only the bull case, at 12%, returns 3.3x-4.4x; the base case at $72M is 1.7x-2.8x, and the bear is 0-1.0x at 50% with the covenant, 35% without it [S53 unverified].

Position sizing is zero at $72M and $6M at $48M-$55M pre-money, with $6M released on 2027 milestones: an independent trial above 85% with bruising no worse than hand-picked fruit, 250 robots contracted at $12,700 or more, a measured v4 unit cost at or below $33,000, and the Calder licence confirmed exclusive after the 100-robot test. The maximum loss is the full $12M; reserve $6M for a Series B. At $50M the assembled $16M round buys 18.18% of the $66M post and returns 2.27x at $150M and 3.79x at $250M (1.77x weighted on $116.8M), against 2.78x at $72M; the full $18M gives 17.65% and 3.68x, a $12M-only close 19.35% and 4.03x. Conditions precedent, not covenants: a Kestrel standstill or waiver signed with the term sheet, licence assignment consent, consolidation of the fleet entity and its grower contracts, and a second board seat with a veto over budgets, debt, related-party contracts and change of control. Diligence next: a firm Tallis quote at 300 units, the Kestrel agreement and UCC filings, the Calder assignment and change-of-control terms, grower contracts and renewal prices, and an insurer's view of product liability [S53, S128].

1. Do not lead at $72M pre-money: 27.7x FY2026E revenue and 51.4x contracted 2027 robot revenue price in the bull case, and Meridian's 13.33% returns 1.67x at a $150M exit, 1.30x on the $116.8M weighted value and 2.78x at $250M [S53 unverified].
2. The investable structure is $48M-$55M pre-money with $6M now and $6M on 2027 milestones; at $50M the assembled $16M round buys 18.18% of the $66M post and returns 3.79x at a $250M exit, while the full $18M gives 17.65% and a $12M-only close 19.35% [S53 unverified].
3. Harvest-level recovery decides the case: 75%-80% makes the machine a harvest aid, while above 85% with clean bruising makes even $72M look cheap [S53 unverified, S56, S181].
